Although these have been treated as separate problems, we show that both are instances of a more fundamental challenge, which we frame as the estimation of semantic distances between SAE features that lie on different activation manifolds. We introduce a distributional framework for this problem, in which each feature is represented not by a single decoder vector like in the literature, but by an activation-weighted distribution over the hidden states that express it. By projecting these distributions into a shared reference space and comparing them with Wasserstein distance, our method provides a unified semantic metric for cross-layer feature comparison. We prove that our representation is invariant to activation rescaling, stable under perturbations, and recovers true matches under finite-sample margin conditions. Empirically, our method outperforms decoder-vector and LLM-based baselines and captures subtle functional distinctions between related features. Notably, our method compresses large feature circuits into interpretable supernodes automatically.

2610.33968:v2.title: Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets
2610.33968:v2.abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are trained to sample objects from compositional spaces with probability proportional to a reward function, but ineffective exploration can cause learned samplers to concentrate on a few high-reward regions. An intuitive remedy is to train multiple GFlowNets independently in parallel and combine their samples. However, this does not prevent multiple models from collapsing onto the same high-reward areas, leaving large regions of the state space unexplored. With this in mind, we propose Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets (HCG), an approach that dynamically partitions the search space to coordinate discovery without relying on hand-crafted boundaries. HCG imposes an ordering in which the highest-ranked model may explore the entire space, while lower-ranked models are progressively pushed toward regions not covered by higher-ranked ones. We provide a theoretical characterization of how specific learning objectives can shift probability mass away from designated areas, instantiating this mechanism within our architecture. A shared classifier coordinates the hierarchy by partitioning the search space, keeping the GFlowNets independently parameterized and enabling asynchronous training. Furthermore, we derive a normalizer-weighted aggregation rule for the ensemble and prove that it recovers the target reward-proportional distribution under the stated assumptions. Finally, experiments across multimodal distributions, sequence generation, combinatorial optimization, and biological sequence design show that HCG improves mode coverage and target approximation, translating increases in the number of coordinated samplers into broader, complementary exploration.

2610.05533:v3.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Three Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
2610.05533:v3.abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit found that the gain came from rows the start left unparsed, that the caller sent each row's reference answer as an assistant turn, and that replication through the same pipeline missed it. Is a harness's gain more than a constant answer would give? We preregistered three studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 7 of 12 cells, mostly on rows the cap left unparsed. It was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells or than four GEPA harnesses at 1.7B. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases (7 fixed by design). At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 points on test but were not detectably above the strongest constant label, and answered "Yes" in 94.6% and 98.2% of parsed mortality answers on test. In the third study (SmolLM3-3B, base Qwen3-1.7B), GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory, both partitions); thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed (the fourth inconclusive on test). On Autocast (exploratory), the harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers, both on test. On questions about the input or about knowledge (FPB, BoolQ, MMLU-Pro), GEPA beat the constant or found no clear gain over thinking off; on questions that ask for a prediction (14B mortality, descriptive; Autocast, exploratory), the harness ended near the constant and gave one label almost throughout while its gain over thinking off looked large. The constant label told the two apart wherever the gain was large. This rests on few tasks that also differ in label skew, number of labels and task type, so it is not shown to depend on the kind of question.

2609.14170:v3.title: Finite-Sample FDR Control for Greedy Aggregation over Networks
2609.14170:v3.abstract: Distributed multiple testing asks $N$ sites, each holding p-values for its own hypotheses, to control the false discovery rate (FDR) of the discoveries made across the whole network while communicating only a small number of bits. Greedy interval aggregation (Pournaderi and Xiang, IEEE TSIPN, 2023) meets the communication budget but controls FDR only asymptotically, and its FDR can exceed the target at finite sample sizes; the same interval counts both select the rejection regions and calibrate the stopping rule, which biases the selected interval densities upward. We propose \emph{budgeted BONuS-GA}: each site mixes synthetic uniform p-values into its data, the center ranks candidate p-value intervals across sites using the pooled counts, and each site's false discoveries are estimated from its own synthetic counts under a per-site share of the level. The procedure needs no knowledge of the null proportions, uses every p-value for both selection and inference, and controls $FDR\leα$ at every sample size for any fixed assignment of hypotheses to sites, assuming only that the null p-values are independent uniforms, independent of the non-null p-values. It keeps the original $O(\sqrt m\log m)$ communication, $m$ being the total number of p-values, when $N=O(\sqrt m)$. We also give a sample-splitting alternative, cross-fit greedy aggregation, with finite-sample control under a random-site model, and we quantify the selection bias behind the original procedure's failure. In a monitoring-network simulation the budgeted procedure retains most of the power of its heuristic counterpart at moderate-to-large site sizes.

2605.23238:v2.title: GENSTRAT: Toward a Science of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
2605.23238:v2.abstract: Fixed game suites for evaluating strategic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) saturate and are hard to keep free of contamination. We introduce GENSTRAT, a system for evaluating the strategic capabilities of LLMs driven by procedural generation of two-player zero-sum imperfect-information betting games, allowing an evaluator to draw novel, fresh games on demand. Each game is characterized on a scale of five complexity axes (state space, temporal contingency, opponent dependence, private information, precision) and measured by Monte Carlo simulation. Using this generator, we construct a 50-game benchmark and hold a tournament of twelve frontier and open-weight models, gathering data from over 40,000 LLM vs. LLM matches. We further construct a composite complexity axis, and find that, on the eight hardest games, the gap between the best and worst model is 1.7x its value across the whole set of games. Ablations show that a higher thinking budget, disclosing the opponent's strategy, and higher reasoning matched to a game's specific demands (for private information and planning depth) were associated with higher margins for the LLM player.

2003.03685:v3.title: Discovering contemporaneous and lagged causal relations in autocorrelated nonlinear time series datasets
2003.03685:v3.abstract: The paper introduces a novel conditional independence (CI) based method for linear and nonlinear, lagged and contemporaneous causal discovery from observational time series in the causally sufficient case. Existing CI-based methods such as the PC algorithm and also common methods from other frameworks suffer from low recall and partially inflated false positives for strong autocorrelation which is an ubiquitous challenge in time series. The novel method, PCMCI$^+$, extends PCMCI [Runge et al., 2019b] to include discovery of contemporaneous links. PCMCI$^+$ improves the reliability of CI tests by optimizing the choice of conditioning sets and even benefits from autocorrelation. The method is order-independent and consistent in the oracle case. A broad range of numerical experiments demonstrates that PCMCI$^+$ has higher adjacency detection power and especially more contemporaneous orientation recall compared to other methods while better controlling false positives. Optimized conditioning sets also lead to much shorter runtimes than the PC algorithm. PCMCI$^+$ can be of considerable use in many real world application scenarios where often time resolutions are too coarse to resolve time delays and strong autocorrelation is present.

2602.00076:v2.title: Repair Brain Damage: Real-Numbered Error Correction Code for Neural Network
2602.00076:v2.abstract: We study neural networks (NNs) operating under hardware-induced memory faults and computational errors, which can degrade reliability in safety-critical applications. To address this challenge, we propose a novel real-valued error correction coding (ECC) framework capable of detecting and correcting both types of errors. Our approach imposes structured real-valued linear constraints on network weights, enabling efficient error detection and recovery without increasing the number of parameters or compromising classification performance. The proposed method leverages linear programming and sparse recovery techniques to achieve low-complexity error correction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-number-based ECC scheme that simultaneously addresses memory and computational errors in neural networks.

2505.14756:v3.title: LLINBO: Trustworthy LLM-in-the-Loop Bayesian Optimization
2505.14756:v3.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sequential decision-making tool widely used for optimizing expensive black-box functions. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable adaptability in low-data regimes, making them promising tools for black-box optimization by leveraging contextual knowledge to propose high-quality query points. However, LLMs lack explicit surrogate modeling and calibrated uncertainty, and their internal mechanisms remain opaque. This structural opacity can result in unnecessary experiments, which are costly in BO and may prevent the search from approaching the optimum. To address this, we propose LLINBO: LLM-in-the-Loop BO, a general framework that wraps existing LLM-based BO approaches, deciding when and how to act on their suggestions and when to revert to classical BO. We introduce three mechanisms for this interaction, each accompanied by a no-harm theoretical guarantee that ensures sublinear cumulative regret for common kernels while requiring no performance assumptions on the LLM. Beyond these theoretical guarantees, we show through simulation studies that LLINBO makes existing LLM-based BO more reliable while still exploiting the LLM's few-shot learning ability to outperform classical BO. We further demonstrate its practical use on a real-world, expensive 3D printing experiment. Code is available at https://github.com/UMDataScienceLab/LLM-in-the-Loop-BO.

2608.19857:v2.title: Inadvertent Context Leakage in Language Models
2608.19857:v2.abstract: For AI agents to be useful beyond simple chat, they must hold sensitive user context such as calendars, credentials, health records, and financial data. We study whether the mere presence of such secrets in a model's context window introduces hidden correlations into the model's benign outputs, allowing reconstruction even when the model correctly refuses direct extraction. We further study whether an adversary can actively engineer prompts that amplify this effect, using the model as a covert carrier to transmit secrets through seemingly innocuous text. In both cases, this limited leakage is exploited using a novel adaptive attack that assumes black-box access to the underlying model. In controlled experiments across eight proprietary models, we find that 2-digit in-context secrets are reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy and 4-digit secrets at 82\% exact match, all from outputs the model produces in response to ordinary, non-adversarial requests. We observe that more capable models leak more: stronger instruction-following amplifies sensitivity to in-context secrets, suggesting leakage is a byproduct of capability as opposed to a patchable bug. We show this leakage enables two practical attacks: (1) a trained classifier that infers semantic predicates about user memories (e.g., health conditions, financial events) from routine natural-language outputs, and (2) an RL-trained adversary that extracts full Social Security Numbers from a production-style agent.

2606.07153:v2.title: No-Harm Physics-Informed Inverse Learning with Residual-Calibrated Uncertainty
2606.07153:v2.abstract: Physics-informed learning is increasingly used for partial differential equation (PDE)-governed inverse problems, but its reliability remains difficult to certify. This paper develops a no-harm certification-and-selection framework for physics-informed inverse learning. A learned reconstruction is accepted only when its residual-calibrated radius is no worse than the baseline radius, namely when $$R_{\mathrm{learn}}\le R_{\mathrm{base}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{safe}};$$otherwise, the method returns the baseline. The certificate combines data, physics, boundary or initial-condition, and optimization residuals. Under a conditional stability estimate, these residuals yield an a posteriori reconstruction-error bound and a deterministic uncertainty radius. A high-probability certificate is also derived for physics residuals estimated from independent random collocation points. Numerical tests on Poisson source recovery, inverse heat reconstruction, limited-angle tomography, elliptic coefficient identification, and stochastic residual validation show that the selector accepts certified improvements, rejects shifted, hallucinated, or unfinished candidates, and becomes conservative in strongly ill-posed regimes. The framework is therefore a certification-and-selection layer, not another reconstruction architecture.

2512.21208:v4.title: A Learning Stability Profile for Finite-Dimensional Learning Dynamics
2512.21208:v4.abstract: We develop a finite-dimensional sensitivity framework for studying stability in learning systems whose states include representations, parameters, and update variables. The central object is the \emph{Learning Stability Profile}, a collection of directional sensitivity operators that records how perturbations in inputs, parameter initialization, and update mechanisms propagate along a specified learning trajectory. The main result is a Lyapunov criterion for controlling this profile. Under explicit regularity, coercivity, and dissipation assumptions, an incremental Lyapunov energy yields uniform or exponentially decaying bounds on the associated linearized transition operators. The result is stated as a sufficient stability criterion, not as an unconditional converse theorem. The framework also distinguishes terminal decay, profile-wise boundedness, and subexponential growth, avoiding the identification of nonpositive growth exponents with uniform boundedness. The profile is then specialized to several standard learning mechanisms. Spectral bounds give forward sensitivity estimates for feedforward networks. Dissipativity and step-size restrictions give stability bounds for residual architectures. Mean-square contraction assumptions yield parameter and update sensitivity bounds for stochastic gradient methods. Locally Lipschitz systems, including piecewise-linear networks, proximal maps, projected updates, and recurrent or state-space recursions, are handled through Clarke generalized Jacobians and variational Lyapunov inequalities. The resulting framework provides a common stability language for architecture, optimization, stochasticity, and nonsmoothness. Its role is structural: it organizes known stability mechanisms within one perturbation calculus while keeping the hypotheses needed for each guarantee explicit.

2511.02496:v3.title: Geometry as a Missing Axis of Representation Quality: The Variational Geometric Information Bottleneck under Data Scarcity
2511.02496:v3.abstract: We study latent geometry as an explicit component of representation quality in data-scarce learning. For an encoder (φ), we define (Q_{β,γ}(φ)=I(φ(X);Y)-β\mathcal C(φ)-γd_{\mathrm{int}}(φ)), combining task-relevant information with penalties for curvature and intrinsic latent dimension. Thus geometry becomes part of the bottleneck criterion, not only a post hoc diagnostic. Under smooth-manifold, loss-transfer, and estimator-concentration assumptions, we derive non-asymptotic low-label generalization bounds where intrinsic dimension and covering complexity enter explicitly. We characterize the information--geometry frontier and prove empirical-surrogate consistency. The analysis links encoder geometry to learning through latent covering numbers, loss-class entropy, and uniform deviation. We instantiate the theory as \texttt{V-GIB}, adding curvature and dimension penalties to variational bottleneck training. Real low-label benchmarks compare \texttt{V-GIB} with ERM, VIB, and ablations across (1%)--(20%) label fractions. Results show improved performance and reduced geometric complexity in several regimes, especially FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10, while confirming that no fixed regularizer is universally dominant.

2602.03514:v3.title: A Function-Space Stability Boundary for Generalization in Interpolating Learning Systems
2602.03514:v3.abstract: Modern learning systems often interpolate training data while still generalizing well, yet it remains unclear when algorithmic stability explains this behavior. We model training as a function-space trajectory and measure sensitivity to single-sample perturbations along this trajectory. We propose a contractive propagation condition and a stability certificate obtained by unrolling the resulting recursion. A small certificate implies stability-based generalization, while we also prove that there exist interpolating regimes with small risk where such contractive sensitivity cannot hold, showing that stability is not a universal explanation. Experiments confirm that certificate growth predicts generalization differences across optimizers, step sizes, and dataset perturbations. The framework therefore identifies regimes where stability explains generalization and where alternative mechanisms must account for success.

2602.01136:v2.title: A Unified Matrix-Spectral Framework for Stability and Interpretability in Deep Learning
2602.01136:v2.abstract: We develop a unified matrix-spectral framework for analyzing stability and interpretability in deep neural networks. Representing networks as data-dependent products of linear operators reveals spectral quantities governing sensitivity to input perturbations, label noise, and training dynamics. We introduce a Global Matrix Stability Index that aggregates spectral information from Jacobians, parameter gradients, Neural Tangent Kernel operators, and loss Hessians into a single stability scale controlling forward sensitivity, attribution robustness, and optimization conditioning. We further show that spectral entropy refines classical operator-norm bounds by capturing typical, rather than purely worst-case, sensitivity. These quantities yield computable diagnostics and stability-oriented regularization principles. Synthetic experiments and controlled studies on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 confirm that modest spectral regularization substantially improves attribution stability even when global spectral summaries change little. The results establish a precise connection between spectral concentration and analytic stability, providing practical guidance for robustness-aware model design and training.

2605.24116:v2.title: Photon Calibration Techniques for High Resolution Cryogenic Detectors
2605.24116:v2.abstract: Monoenergetic photons from a pulsed laser diode or LED are commonly used to calibrate the detector response of high-resolution calorimetric detectors. However, when the detector's resolution is larger than the energy of a single photon, a calibration is normally derived using Poisson statistics. In this paper, we clarify the assumptions implicit in this calibration method, before considering how a more realistic model of a detector's performance will violate these assumptions, biasing the calibration. Finally, we judge the individual impact of specific detector parameters on our calibration, and conclude with discussion of both the limits of our calculations and the implications for state-of-the art detectors.

2610.11748:v2.title: DEX: Digit-Level Early Exit for Energy-Efficient MSDF Neural Network Inference
2610.11748:v2.abstract: U-Net inference for brain-tumor segmentation requires billions of multiply-accumulate operations, motivating hardware that can reduce computation dynamically rather than relying only on fixed precision or static model compression. Most-significant-digit-first (MSDF) arithmetic exposes the leading digits of a result during computation, enabling output-dependent decisions before the full value is generated. This paper presents an MSDF accelerator for quantized U-Net segmentation with a two-stage grouped processing element supporting signed INT8 operands and in-stream bias accumulation. Four runtime mechanisms operate directly on the output digit stream: exact early negative detection (END) in ReLU layers, exact sign-only decision making in the segmentation head, calibrated low-order-digit skipping, and calibrated pruning. The two approximate mechanisms are selected offline under an accuracy constraint, while execution requires only lightweight control and does not modify the stored weights. On a residual U-Net trained with nnU-Net for BraTS, the proposed mechanisms reduce digit cycles by 38.38\% while achieving a mean Dice score of 80.58\% on 73 held-out cases, compared with 81.20\% for the floating-point model; the exact mechanisms alone reduce cycles by 18.79\% without altering the quantized output. Synthesized in 45~nm, the processing element operates at 500~MHz, occupies 0.858~mm$^2$, and consumes 0.726~mJ per $192\times192$ patch under switching-activity-annotated power analysis. A projected eight-output accelerator with shared activation delivery achieves 16.6~ms latency and 1.67~mJ per patch.

2609.07990:v2.title: HyCO: A Hybrid Neural Solver for Combinatorial Optimization
2609.07990:v2.abstract: Sequential reinforcement learning (RL) solvers and global diffusion model (DM) solvers for neural combinatorial optimization exhibit complementary failure modes under an optimization-regret view. The former enjoys small marginal regret in the early construction stage, but suffers from horizon-wise compounding errors with super-linear regret growth; the latter avoids horizon compounding but incurs linear or sublinear regret w.r.t. the dimension of the remaining unsolved subspace. We propose Hybrid Neural Solver for Combinatorial Optimization (HyCO), a hybrid inference algorithm that constructs a solution prefix with an RL solver and adaptively switches to a conditional DM to complete the remaining decisions. To characterize why such hybridization helps, when to trigger the handover, and how to realize it in practice, we first develop a unified error-scaling theoretical framework and prove that, under explicit error-scaling assumptions, i) the hybrid structure achieves strictly lower expected regret than either backbone alone, and ii) there exists a unique optimal trigger step that minimizes the hybrid regret. We then design a lightweight adaptive trigger that combines policy entropy and RL-DM disagreement to detect trajectory-level signals of the regime shift as a practical proxy, since the optimal trigger step is defined at the expected-regret level and is not directly computable on individual trajectories. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that HyCO achieves consistent improvements over both backbones and support the empirical effectiveness of adaptive triggering. Our code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/wmd3i/HyCO.

2605.12388:v3.title: Events as Triggers for Behavioral Diversity in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
2605.12388:v3.abstract: Effective multi-agent cooperation requires agents to adopt diverse behaviors as task conditions evolve-and to do so at the right moment. Yet, current Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) frameworks that facilitate this diversity are still limited by the fact that they bind fixed behaviors to fixed agent identities. Consequently, they are ill-equipped for tasks where agents need to take on different roles at very specific moments in time. We argue that, to define these behavioral transitions, the missing ingredient is $\textbf{events}$. Events are changes in the state of the system that induce qualitative changes in the task. Based on this view, we introduce a framework that decouples agent identity from behavior, capturing a continuous manifold from which agents instantiate their behaviors in response to events. This framework is based on two elements. First, to build an expressive behavior manifold, we introduce Neural Manifold Diversity (NMD), a formal distance metric that remains well-defined when behaviors are transient and agent-agnostic. Second, we use an event-based hypernetwork that generates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules over a shared team policy, enabling on-the-fly agent-policy reconfiguration in response to events. We prove that this construction ensures that diversity does not interfere with reward maximization by design. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework outperforms established baselines across benchmarks while exhibiting zero-shot generalization, and being the only method that solves tasks requiring sequential behavior reassignment.

2606.10668:v2.title: $Λ$(1520) as a probe of resonance-driven deuteron formation at the LHC
2606.10668:v2.abstract: Light nuclei such as deuterons are produced abundantly in high-energy proton-proton and nuclear collisions despite their tiny binding energies. Their production mechanism remains unresolved, as both nucleon coalescence and statistical thermal models reproduce inclusive LHC yields. We propose a direct invariant-mass observable that discriminates between these scenarios using the long-lived $Λ(1520) \to {\rm pK}$ resonance. If decay protons coalesce into deuterons, the produced nuclei remain correlated with the kaon, allowing the resonance peak to be reconstructed experimentally through proxy masses, $M_{\rm (d/2)K}$, formed from kaons and half the deuteron four-momentum. Using Thermal-FIST and PYTHIA with a deuteron coalescence afterburner, we show that a $M_{\rm (d/2)K}$ peak emerges only in the coalescence scenario. This observable provides a direct experimental probe of resonance-fed deuteron production and of late-stage coalescence dynamics in high-energy collisions.

2608.25182:v2.title: Minimax Alternating Regret for the Experts Problem and Online Convex Optimization
2608.25182:v2.abstract: In this paper, we study alternating regret in online convex optimization (OCO), motivated by the success of alternating learning dynamics in two-player games. Although previous works have shown that $o(\sqrt{T})$ alternating regret is achievable under various assumptions on the loss functions and feasible domains, the minimax regret rate has remained open even for the expert problem. In this paper, we resolve this question by showing matching lower and upper bounds for both the expert problem and general OCO. Somewhat surprisingly, for the $d$-expert problem, we show that the minimax alternating regret is $Θ(\log d)$ by providing both a lower bound and an algorithm achieving a matching upper bound. This significantly improves upon the $O(T^{1/3}\log^{2/3} d)$ established by [HLLZ25]. We further extend our results to general OCO over a $d$-dimensional compact convex set and prove that the worst-case minimax alternating regret is $Θ\left(d\log \left(1+\frac{T}{d}\right)\right)$, also significantly improving upon the $O((d\log T)^{2/3}T^{1/3})$ upper bound and resolving the open problem posed by [CCK+23,HLLZ25]. As a direct implication, our alternating dynamics achieve $O(\frac{\log d}{T})$ convergence to Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games, matching the state of the art, and give the first such convergence rate to coarse correlated equilibrium in two-player general-sum games. Technically, our upper bound for the expert problem is achieved by a corrected variant of Hedge. We extend the same corrected-potential argument to continuous action sets to obtain the optimal alternating-regret rate for OCO. For the lower bounds, the construction for the expert problem repeatedly eliminates half of the candidate experts, while the OCO lower bound instance construction replaces this discrete elimination by a more involved multiscale construction on the unit disk.

2604.06558:v2.title: When Does Context Help? A Systematic Study of Target-Conditional Molecular Property Prediction
2604.06558:v2.abstract: We present the first systematic study of when target context helps molecular property prediction, evaluating context conditioning across 10 diverse protein families, 4 fusion architectures, data regimes spanning 67-9,409 training compounds, and both temporal and random evaluation splits. Using NestDrug, a FiLM-based architecture that conditions molecular representations on target identity, we characterize both success and failure modes with three principal findings. First, fusion architecture dominates: FiLM outperforms concatenation by 24.2 percentage points and additive conditioning by 8.6 pp; how you incorporate context matters more than whether you include it. Second, context enables otherwise impossible predictions: on data-scarce CYP3A4 (67 training compounds), multi-task transfer achieves 0.686 AUC where per-target Random Forest collapses to 0.238. Third, context can systematically hurt: distribution mismatch causes 10.2 pp degradation on BACE1; few-shot adaptation consistently underperforms zero-shot. Beyond methodology, we expose fundamental flaws in standard benchmarking: 1-nearest-neighbor Tanimoto achieves 0.991 AUC on DUD-E without any learning, and 50% of actives leak from training data, rendering absolute performance metrics meaningless. Our temporal split evaluation (train up to 2020, test 2021-2024) achieves stable 0.843 AUC with no degradation, providing the first rigorous evidence that context-conditional molecular representations generalize to future chemical space.

2605.27954:v2.journal_ref: Published at Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026
2605.27954:v2.title: Cyclical Entropy Eruption: Entropy Dynamics in Agent Reinforcement Learning
2605.27954:v2.abstract: Agentic large language models are increasingly used to solve real-world tasks by reasoning over goals, invoking tools, and interacting with external environments. Reinforcement learning provides a natural framework for improving these behaviors, and recent agent RL methods have achieved strong results across domains. However, the training dynamics of agent RL remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to diagnose instabilities and design more effective training algorithms. In this work, we identify a previously underexplored phenomenon in agent RL, which we term cyclical entropy eruption. Unlike single-turn reasoning RL, where entropy typically collapses and stays low, agent RL training exhibits unique recurring cycles of sharp entropy eruption and gradual subsidence. We decompose this dynamic into three phases and provide theoretical and empirical analyses of each, explaining the mechanisms underlying its cyclical oscillation. We further show that degenerate patterns such as sentence duplication and hallucination, once acquired during eruption, can persist and accumulate across cycles. Motivated by these findings, we propose SEAL (Separation-Enhanced Agent Learning), a lightweight auxiliary loss that separates correct and incorrect trajectories in representation space, directly targeting the root cause of entropy eruption. Experiments across multiple benchmarks, models, and RL algorithms demonstrate that SEAL stabilizes training and yields stronger downstream agent performance.

2601.17986:v2.title: Federated learning for unpaired multimodal data
2601.17986:v2.abstract: Training of multimodal foundation models is currently restricted to centralized data centers containing massive, aligned datasets (e.g., image-text pairs). However, in realistic federated environments, data is often unpaired and fragmented across disjoint nodes; one node may hold sensor data, while another holds textual logs. These datasets are strictly private and share no common samples. Current federated learning (FL) methods fail in this regime, as they assume local clients possess aligned pairs or require sharing raw feature embeddings, which violates data sovereignty. We propose a novel framework to train a global multimodal transformer across decentralized nodes with disjoint modalities. We introduce a small public anchor set to align disjoint private manifolds. Using Gram matrices calculated from these public anchors, we enforce semantic alignment across modalities through centered kernel alignment without ever transmitting private samples, offering a mathematically superior privacy guarantee compared to prototype sharing. Further, we introduce a subspace-stabilized fine-tuning method to handle FL with huge transformer models. We strictly decouple domain-specific magnitude shifts from semantic direction, ensuring that nodes with varying sensor characteristics align geometrically to the global consensus. Lastly, we propose precision weighted averaging, where efficiently obtained uncertainty estimates are used to downweight uncertain nodes. This paper establishes the mathematical backbone for federated unpaired foundation models, enabling a global model to learn a unified representation of the world from fragmented, disjoint, and private data silos without requiring centralized storage or paired samples.

2610.37239:v2.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning
2610.37239:v2.abstract: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.

2506.13554:v3.title: Non-Asymptotic Stability and Consistency Guarantees for Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Coercive Operator Analysis
2506.13554:v3.abstract: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing the stability and consistency of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), grounded in operator coercivity, variational formulations, and non-asymptotic perturbation theory. PINNs approximate solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) by minimizing residual losses over sampled collocation and boundary points. We formalize both operator-level and variational notions of consistency, proving that residual minimization in Sobolev norms leads to convergence in energy and uniform norms under mild regularity. Deterministic stability bounds quantify how bounded perturbations to the network outputs propagate through the full composite loss, while probabilistic concentration results via McDiarmid's inequality yield sample complexity guarantees for residual-based generalization. A unified generalization bound links residual consistency, projection error, and perturbation sensitivity. Empirical results on elliptic, parabolic, and nonlinear PDEs confirm the predictive accuracy of our theoretical bounds across regimes. The framework identifies key structural principles, such as operator coercivity, activation smoothness, and sampling admissibility, that underlie robust and generalizable PINN training, offering principled guidance for the design and analysis of PDE-informed learning systems.

2603.12183:v3.title: Proof-Carrying Materials: Falsifiable Safety Certificates for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
2603.12183:v3.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are deployed for high-throughput materials screening without formal reliability guarantees. We show that a single MLIP used as a stability filter misses 93% of density functional theory (DFT)-stable materials (recall 0.07) on a 25,000-material benchmark. Proof-Carrying Materials (PCM) closes this gap through three stages: adversarial falsification across compositional space, bootstrap envelope refinement with 95% confidence intervals, and Lean 4 formal certification. Auditing CHGNet, TensorNet and MACE reveals architecture-specific blind spots with near-zero pairwise error correlations (r <= 0.13; n = 5,000), confirmed by independent Quantum ESPRESSO validation (20/20 converged; median DFT/CHGNet force ratio 12x). A risk model trained on PCM-discovered features predicts failures on unseen materials (AUC-ROC = 0.938 +/- 0.004) and transfers across architectures (cross-MLIP AUC-ROC ~ 0.70; feature importance r = 0.877). In a thermoelectric screening case study, PCM-audited protocols discover 62 additional stable materials missed by single-MLIP screening - a 25% improvement in discovery yield.

2609.13547:v2.title: Toward Optimal Switching Regret for Multi-Armed Bandits with Oblivious Adversary
2609.13547:v2.abstract: We study switching regret in adversarial multi-armed bandits, where the learner competes with an arm sequence that changes at most $S$ times. When $S$ is known, an optimal expected regret of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{(S+1)KT})$ is obtainable [Auer et al., 2002]. However, when $S$ is unknown, Marinov and Zimmert [2021] show that this guarantee is impossible under an adaptive adversary. In this paper, we show that a single algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{(S+1)KT})$ expected regret for every $S$ against an oblivious adversary, resolving an open problem of Auer et al. [2019b]. Our algorithm combines a fixed-share learner initialized with a small learning rate and dyadic-interval subroutines that search for local improvements using randomized learning rates and implicit exploration. Importantly, a non-uniform prior favors following the main learner, keeping the cost of maintaining many subroutines small. When the subroutines accumulate sufficient improvement over the main learner, its learning rate doubles, allowing adaptation to the unknown number of comparator switches $S$.

2502.03604:v4.title: Bilevel ZOFO: Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning and Meta-Training
2502.03604:v4.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) for downstream tasks using First-Order (FO) optimizers presents significant computational challenges. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods address these by freezing most model parameters and training only a small subset. However, PEFT often underperforms compared to full fine-tuning when high task-specific accuracy is required. Zeroth-Order (ZO) methods fine-tune the entire pre-trained model without back-propagation, estimating gradients through forward passes only. While memory-efficient, ZO methods suffer from slow convergence and high sensitivity to prompt selection. We bridge these two worlds with Bilevel-ZOFO, a bilevel optimization method that couples fast, local FO-PEFT adaptation at the inner level with stable, memory-efficient ZO updates of the full backbone at the outer level. The FO-PEFT inner loop performs fast, low-memory local adaptation that reduces the variance of ZO estimates and stabilizes the search, guiding the outer ZO updates of the full backbone and reducing prompt sensitivity. In the mean time, the outer ZO provides better generalization ability for PEFT. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees and empirically demonstrate that Bilevel-ZOFO significantly outperforms existing ZO and FO-PEFT methods, achieving 2-4 times faster training while maintaining similar memory efficiency. Additionally, we show by updating the backbone with ZO and adapting only a tiny FO-PEFT block per task, Bilevel-ZOFO combines full-model capacity with few-shot efficiency, making it a very efficient meta-learning algorithm that quickly adapts to new tasks.

2607.04449:v2.title: Fields of the Planet: Field Boundary Mapping Beyond 10m
2607.04449:v2.abstract: Field-boundary accuracy depends on the model, sensor resolution, label discretization, and evaluation procedure. Measuring the contribution of sensor resolution therefore requires a controlled comparison across sensors. We present Fields of the Planet (FTP), a 3 m PlanetScope companion to Fields of The World (FTW) containing 133,168 co-registered patch-window targets across 24 countries. FTP preserves FTW's vector polygons, seasonal windows, and dataset splits, enabling direct comparison with 10 m Sentinel-2. We first quantify the resolution ceiling by rasterizing and vectorizing the same ground-truth parcels at each resolution to determine which fields the label grid can represent. We evaluate predicted parcels with polygon-level and boundary metrics. With identical PRUE+ training and post-processing across sensors, plus an upsampled Sentinel-2 control, we isolate gains from image content. PlanetScope raises panoptic quality (PQ) from 21.0 to 35.5, improves PQ on sub-$0.5$ ha fields from 5.8 to 15.7, and reduces matched-boundary error from 18.6 m to 7.4 m. Pixel-level metrics understate this improvement, so field-boundary benchmarks should account for sensor resolution.

2602.01418:v3.title: Parabolic Positional Encoding: A Vision-Centric, Principled, Extrapolatable, and General Approach
2602.01418:v3.abstract: We propose Parabolic Positional Encoding (PaPE), a parabola-based positional encoding for vision modalities in attention-based architectures. Given a set of vision tokens-such as from videos, event camera streams, images, or point clouds-our objective is to encode their positions while accounting for the characteristics of vision modalities. Prior works have largely extended positional encodings from 1D-sequences in language to nD-structures in vision, but only with partial account of vision characteristics. We address this gap by designing PaPE from principles distilled from prior work: translation invariance, rotation invariance (PaPE-RI), distance decay, directionality, and context awareness. Extrapolation experiments on ImageNet-1K show how PaPE extrapolates remarkably well, improving in absolute terms by up to 10.5 over the next-best encoding. Generality experiments on 8 datasets across 4 modalities show that PaPE is a general vision positional encoding, as PaPE matches the best baseline on 5 datasets and exceeds all on 2 datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/DTU-PAS/parabolic-position-encoding.

2608.14465:v2.title: You Only Pass Once: Answering and Abstaining Together in a Single Forward Pass of a Frozen Language Model
2608.14465:v2.abstract: A frozen language model under-uses the evidence in its hidden states and answers confidently when the context contains no answer. We fix both on the residual stream without changing any weight. For accuracy, a small trained network (the probe) adds an input-dependent vector to the residual at several middle layers; it raises Qwen2.5-1.5B on $α$NLI from 51% to 73% accuracy. For abstention, a fixed vector (the direction), the mean hidden state of contexts that contain the answer minus that of contexts that do not, scores the hidden state; a low score abstains. On four QA datasets with human answerability labels (Qwen2.5-7B), moving the direction to a dataset it was not fit on costs under 3 points of decision accuracy (from 0.83 in domain) on average and still beats asking the model whether its context suffices; the same judgment trained as a classifier into the probe's activation edit or into LoRA weights loses 16 and 22 points and ends below asking. We set out to put both functions on a single forward pass, and found that the probe's edit changes the very hidden state the direction scores, degrading it. A small map -- trained without labels, only to reconstruct the unedited hidden state from the edited one -- removes 63% of that interference on 1.5B. Refit on the hidden-state pairs of LoFiT or LoReFT, the same recipe repairs those methods too: the steering module is replaceable. The resulting system, YOPO, answers and abstains in one forward pass. On $α$NLI it raises three-way accuracy from 0.38 to about 0.75 on 1.5B, and stays within 0.02 of a two-pass reference on 1.5B, 3B and 7B, at half the cost. We also observe improvements on the four QA datasets, where answerability is human-labeled and answers are generated as free-form text. Near-parity with the two-pass reference holds across nine backbones spanning six model families without backbone-specific hyperparameter tuning.

2610.29641:v2.title: Recursive Code Evolution for Task-Oriented Semantic Communications
2610.29641:v2.abstract: Semantic communication jointly optimizes inference accuracy, channel use, and computation, yet the underlying communication program is typically specified before training. This paper presents ComRSI (Communications-Oriented Recursive Self-Improvement), a framework for recursively evolving that program through large-language-model-assisted code edits. An agent modifies the encoder, channel adapters, decoder, loss, and training policy; a protected evaluator screens candidates under prescribed budgets and resource constraints. Accepted code and textual feedback inform subsequent proposals, while candidate weights are trained from scratch. In the original ten-generation CIFAR-100 lineage, eight accepted revisions produce an attention-pooled code achieving 74.3% test accuracy over an Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel at 32 complex symbols per image, compared with 67.2% at 256 symbols for the initial design. The program also improves fading-channel accuracy and transfers to Tiny-ImageNet after retraining, where a separate ComRSI search demonstrates further recursive improvements. A repeat study with ten searches per method compares ComRSI against non-recursive agents with and without textual history. Mean final search scores balancing accuracy, transmission rate, and computational cost are 0.7587, 0.7376, and 0.7089, respectively; the mean numbers of accepted revisions per search are 6.0, 5.0, and 2.1. The advantage over the memoryless agent is supported by a two-sided rank test, whereas the difference from the history-equipped agent remains statistically inconclusive at this sample size. Archived proposals show that pooling can yield a large improvement, while retained history supports subsequent refinement. These results support recursive program optimization within the evaluated setting and expose its remaining rate-robustness and compute-placement trade-offs.

2610.29262:v2.title: Estimating Performance for Safe Deployment of Machine Learning Models
2610.29262:v2.abstract: The main challenge in applying deep neural networks to real-world scenarios lies in distributional discrepancies between training and test datasets, often caused by variations in data acquisition conditions. Assessing the performance of pre-trained models without labels is crucial for safety, but this is complicated by deep models' overly optimistic probabilistic outputs, often exacerbated by class imbalances, leading to unreliable predictions. To address these issues, we introduce MOVAL, a novel MOdel eVALuation tool that estimates performance using unlabeled test data. MOVAL incorporates class-wise confidence calibration to adjust model outputs, allowing for the estimation of metrics beyond accuracy and mitigating the detrimental effects of class imbalance on confidence calibration. Additionally, we propose an ensemble approach that combines multiple calibrated confidence scores for a more robust solution. We validate MOVAL on natural and medical image datasets with various acquisition shifts, covering tasks from classification to segmentation. It achieves state-of-the-art results across evaluation metrics such as accuracy, F1-Score, AUC, and more. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MOVAL provides accurate performance estimations at the class, instance, and pixel levels, ensuring the transparent and safe deployment of machine learning models. We provide MOVAL as a deployment tool for monitoring and estimating performance under a range of domain shifts.

2608.26538:v2.title: Predicting Dose-Response Success from Primary Screening Data
2608.26538:v2.abstract: High-throughput drug screening uses inexpensive primary screens to select compounds for more costly follow-up dose-response experiments, which estimate compound potency (pXC50) by determining the concentration required to produce a specified biological effect. However, many promoted compounds fail to yield a reportable potency, even when activity is subsequently confirmed. We investigated whether inexpensive three-point primary-screening data could predict whether a more costly 11-point dose-response experiment would yield a reportable pXC50. Using a dataset of 32,971 compound-assay pairs with three-point primary-screening and 11-point dose-response measurements, we trained random-forest models to predict successful potency quantification. Our model achieved an AUROC of 0.939 +/- 0.002 and generalized to previously unseen chemical scaffolds and assay-mechanism families. We found that primary-screen response features were more predictive of dose-response quantifiability than molecular structure-based features. Successful potency quantification was also strongly associated with primary-screen response amplitude. Across eight chronological test releases, the model retrospectively retained 90% of reportable potencies while selecting only 55.7% of historically promoted compound-assay pairs for follow-up profiling. These findings suggest that predicting potency quantifiability from primary-screening data could improve the efficiency of compound prioritization and reduce unnecessary dose-response experiments.

2610.34422:v2.title: From GPU to TPU with Coding Agents: What Works, What Fails, and What It Costs?
2610.34422:v2.abstract: A coding agent can migrate a machine learning workload, report success, and still change how the model trains. Rising compute costs, limited accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence are pushing organizations toward alternatives to graphics processing units (GPUs); a key question is whether agent-generated migrations to tensor processing units (TPUs) can be trusted and at what cost. We build a dataset of 148 PyTorch ML research projects and use Claude Code to migrate ten of them from NVIDIA GPUs to Google Cloud TPUs. We independently assess whether each migration runs, preserves numerical behavior, executes on the intended hardware, maintains the project's goal, and delivers acceptable performance. We also examine failures, human effort, and costs. Eight projects meet our project-goal criterion, and migrations require 2.4 human interventions on average. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 fail (76%), and 26 of these failures (49%) raise no error. The most frequent cause is repeated compilation and other execution inefficiencies, while interactions with third-party libraries can silently change the computation: in one four-chip migration, the agent reports success despite a change in gradient clipping that reduces accuracy from 86.53% to 84.89%. Execution costs vary widely: in one workload, TorchTPU, a PyTorch execution backend for TPUs, trains 1.86 times faster and 25% cheaper per run than the GPU. For practitioners, these findings motivate independent reference runs, verification under the intended hardware configuration, and workload-specific acceptance and stopping criteria that account for both computational and human costs.

2610.22283:v3.title: Learning the information contained in the microstructure of data distributions
2610.22283:v3.abstract: Understanding how much and where information is nested in sets of data obtained using different parameters and metrics is a typical problem in the analysis of high-dimensional datasets. Approaches based on relative data-driven metrics may be poorly quantitative and difficult to interpret, while accurate methods may be computationally expensive and impractical for large datasets. Here, we report an efficient, quantitative, and transferable method useful to this end, which we call "Micro-Information Analysis". Its foundation is based on the tight relationship that exists between the microscopic features of data distributions and the information they contain. The method performs preliminary unsupervised clustering, capturing microstructural features of data distributions such as the dominant Gaussian microdomains (microstates) present in them, their population, separation, and their residual non-Gaussian fraction. Leveraging the principle of clustering-and-minimization of Shannon entropy, this allows quantifying in bit (that is, in absolute metric) the information contained in the microstructure of the data, and how much information is nested in each Gaussian and non-Gaussian microdomain. The output of the analysis is a set of easily interpretable Information-Microstructure plots that allow to readily compare and rank data based on their information content and to graphically map the information breakdown among their various microenvironments in diagrams that are easy to interpret. We prove the efficiency of our method by analyzing and ranking data generated synthetically or from molecular simulations, demonstrating how "Micro-Information Analysis" is a physically-grounded quantitative tool useful for the study of physical systems from their data and for data science in general.

2607.23607:v2.title: MS-GPT: Rethinking MS/MS De Novo Structure Elucidation as Spectrum-Induced Posterior Querying of a Molecule-Language Model
2607.23607:v2.abstract: Molecular structure elucidation from tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) is a central inverse problem in analytical chemistry. Most existing approaches to MS/MS identification remain tied to reference libraries or predefined candidate sets, whereas de novo methods aim to generate structures directly from spectra. A common de novo route predicts a molecular fingerprint from the spectrum and then decodes structures from it, enabling decoder pretraining on large molecule-only corpora. However, this paradigm creates a training-inference mismatch: the decoder is trained on oracle fingerprints computed from molecules, but at inference it is queried with a noisy spectrum-induced fingerprint posterior that is typically collapsed to a single thresholded fingerprint. We introduce MS-GPT, which recasts fingerprint-mediated de novo elucidation as spectrum-induced posterior querying of a conditional molecule-language model. MS-GPT conditions a molecule-language model on fingerprints and formulas, then converts the spectrum-induced posterior into a band of fingerprint queries near the oracle-fingerprint manifold through active-bit density calibration. Candidates sampled across this band are pooled and ranked by generation frequency and posterior similarity. A lightweight LoRA adapter further mitigates domain-specific posterior bias while preserving the pretrained molecular prior. On NPLIB1 and MassSpecGym, MS-GPT sets a new state of the art, reaching Top-1/Top-10 exact-match accuracy of 17.1%/27.6% and 10.2%/13.2%, respectively, and candidate-pool scaling improves recovery with a near-linear increase in inference cost. The source code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/VIKI623/MS-GPT.

2610.09096:v2.title: Are We Really Benchmarking Forecasting Models? The Impact of Preprocessing on Time Series Performance
2610.09096:v2.abstract: While established literature underscores the pivotal role of preprocessing in forecasting accuracy, this stage remains largely overlooked in current research. Modern benchmarks typically resort to simple scaling, failing to account for critical transformations required to address nonstationarity, such as differencing. This omission creates a significant structural preprocessing bias that favors models with built-in data treatments while obscuring the true potential of simpler architectures. We study this effect through a preprocessing-aware benchmark that evaluates 11 forecasting models across 16 reversible preprocessing pipelines on 29,000 M4 time series. Our results identify preprocessing as a key driver of forecasting performance. Optimizing preprocessing per series yields gains of approximately 27\% to 87\% across all evaluated models, with architectures lacking internalized preprocessing experiencing the most substantial improvements. This allows simpler architectures to become highly competitive with complex, state-of-the-art models in modern forecasting benchmarks. All resources and experimental results from this benchmark are stored in a comprehensive metadataset to support future metalearning tasks.
authors: Paulo S. G. de Mattos Neto

2610.37381:v2.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
2610.37381:v2.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.

2605.25592:v3.title: Optimal Design for Multinomial Logit Model with Applications to Best Assortment Identification
2605.25592:v3.abstract: We study optimal experimental design for multinomial logit (MNL) bandits, where an agent repeatedly selects a subset of $K$ items from a ground set of size $N$ and observes single-choice feedback. Unlike linear or generalized linear bandits, MNL bandits have a combinatorial action space, which makes classical optimal design approaches and naive optimization over all subsets computationally intractable. We propose a computationally efficient optimal design framework for MNL models that achieves both statistical efficiency and scalability through two complementary approaches: (i) an exact or certified-approximate reformulation of the design oracle as a $0$-$1$ mixed-integer linear program (MILP) with solver-certified early stopping, and (ii) a fully polynomial-time lifted design that replaces the nonlinear objective with a tractable surrogate. Using the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem, we establish near G-optimality guarantees and characterize the induced statistical-computational trade-offs. As an application, we develop a best assortment identification algorithm for MNL bandits with linear utilities and non-uniform revenues, and prove an instance-dependent sample complexity of $\tilde{O}\big(\frac{d \log N}{Δ^2}\big)$, where $d$ is the feature dimension, $N$ is the number of arms, and $Δ$ is the minimum revenue gap.

2408.17246:v3.title: Learning Maximal Regions of Attraction on Compact Sets using Taylor Lyapunov Networks
2408.17246:v3.abstract: We consider the problem of learning maximal Lyapunov functions to compute the maximal region of attraction of nonlinear dynamical systems using neural networks. Two obstacles limit existing neural-network approaches: 1) finite-width approximations can fail to preserve the strict Lyapunov inequalities near the equilibrium, where they become arbitrarily weak, and 2) training is necessarily performed on a bounded computational domain for which the classical Lyapunov and Zubov theorems do not directly apply. To address these issues, first we derive Lyapunov and Zubov theorems directly on a prescribed compact computational domain, characterizing the maximal region of attraction within that domain as the solution of a boundary-value PDE. Second, we introduce the Taylor Lyapunov network, an architecture that prescribes the quadratic leading-order term via the system's linearization and represents the higher-order remainder through a structured cubic factorization, guaranteeing that any network in this class is a valid local Lyapunov function by construction. Finally, we prove that Taylor Lyapunov networks are universal approximators of maximal Lyapunov functions on compact domains, and combine these results into an unsupervised, physics-informed training procedure. Numerical experiments on systems of varying dimensions and stability types show that the proposed architecture is efficient at estimating the maximum region of attraction.

2611.03152:v1.title: From PID to Reinforcement Learning in Building HVAC Control: A Control-Architecture Review of Tuning Strategies, Formulations, and Deployment Trade-offs
2611.03152:v1.abstract: This paper reviews control architectures for building heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, addressing the tension among energy demand, occupant comfort and equipment operability, and situating proportional-integral-derivative (PID) regulation within a layered control stack that also includes rule-based and model-based supervisory control and data-driven reinforcement learning (RL). It examines the thermostat-PID layer from two-position and scheduled setpoint control through proportional, PI and PID regulation and their tuning, then formulates RL for building control as a Markov decision process. Its central contribution is a taxonomy of where RL meets PID: RL as a gain tuner for an existing loop, as a direct replacement for the regulatory controller, as a hybrid with model predictive control, and as supervisory setpoint and schedule generation. Across these classes, the review establishes that the physical loop remains invariant while the intervention point changes, and that the classes differ in their requirements for actuation authority, state information, modelling, commissioning and constraint handling. It further establishes that PID is inexpensive and well codified but limited by nonlinearity, time variation, discrete mode switching, loop interaction and slow plant dynamics, while RL's admissible position must be argued rather than assumed. The paper concludes that these architectures are not competing philosophies of control but nested points of attachment on one HVAC plant, with hybrid implementations possible, and that deployment trade-offs must be assessed according to the specific control interface and scaffolding required.

2611.03150:v1.journal_ref: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
2611.03150:v1.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
2611.03150:v1.abstract: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.

2611.03146:v1.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
2611.03146:v1.abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.

2610.33004:v2.title: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription
2610.33004:v2.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is essential for digitizing historical archives, yet standard evaluation metrics such as Character Error Rate (CER) do not necessarily reflect whether meaningful information, such as names, dates, and identifiers, is preserved. In this work, we investigate entitylevel analysis of OCR errors as a complementary perspective for evaluating OCR quality in historical documents. Using a publicly available benchmark of 175 documents from the Berrutti Archive, augmented with 5,209 manually annotated entity mentions that will be released upon acceptance, we compare sequence-recognition OCR systems, OCR-specialized vision-language models, and general-purpose vision-language models. Beyond global transcription accuracy, we analyze entity preservation and recoverability under varying character-level edit tolerances. Our experiments show that OCR rankings depend on the evaluation criterion: while Qwen 3.6 achieves the highest entity coverage across all tested tolerances, several systems with lower exact-match coverage recover substantially when small errors are tolerated, suggesting that many of their errors correspond to localized character-level deviations rather than fundamentally incorrect entity transcriptions. Conversely, some systems remain unable to recover many entities even under relaxed matching. These findings show that OCR quality cannot be fully characterized by aggregate transcription metrics alone and highlight the importance of evaluating how OCR errors affect the preservation and recoverability of meaningful information.

2506.03234:v2.title: The Alignment Illusion: How BadReward Corrupts Text-to-Image Generation
2506.03234:v2.abstract: Modern text-to-image generative models increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to align generated content with human preferences and safety standards. This post-training stage is critical for optimizing models toward high-fidelity and value-aligned behaviors using human preference data. However, while previous works have extensively investigated poisoning attacks against the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage of text-to-image training, the security vulnerabilities introduced by the RLHF process remain unexplored. In this paper, we present the first exploration into the feasibility of poisoning the RLHF process as a novel attack surface for compromising text-to-image models. We introduce BadReward, an indirect clean-label poisoning attack that manipulates reward signals to embed malicious behaviors. Our approach leverages a feature collision mechanism to produce poison preference image pairs that are visually benign, but aligned with a malicious target concept in the reward feature space. Our experiments demonstrate that this manipulation effectively corrupts the reward signal. Online RLHF further amplifies this corruption through its reward-model feedback loop, whereas offline preference optimization learns directly from the poisoned preferences. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world effectiveness of BadReward on modern text-to-image architectures, showing high attack success rates and visual stealthiness across different RLHF algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJUICSR/BadReward.

2604.19009:v2.title: Guiding Distribution Matching Distillation with Gradient-Based Reinforcement Learning
2604.19009:v2.abstract: Diffusion distillation, exemplified by Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), has shown great promise in few-step generation but often sacrifices quality for sampling speed. While integrating Reinforcement Learning (RL) into distillation offers potential, a naive fusion of these two objectives relies on suboptimal raw sample evaluation. This sample-based scoring creates inherent conflicts with the distillation trajectory and produces unreliable rewards due to the noisy nature of early-stage generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose GDMD, a novel framework that redefines the reward mechanism by prioritizing distillation gradients over raw pixel outputs as the primary signal for optimization. By reinterpreting the DMD gradients as implicit target tensors, our framework enables existing reward models to directly evaluate the quality of distillation updates. This gradient-level guidance functions as an adaptive weighting that synchronizes the RL policy with the distillation objective, effectively neutralizing optimization divergence. Empirical results show that GDMD sets a new SOTA for few-step generation. Specifically, our 4-step models outperform the quality of their multi-step teacher and substantially exceed previous DMDR results in GenEval and human-preference metrics, exhibiting strong scalability potential.

2611.03117:v1.title: Inner optimizers in active-learning Kriging reliability analysis: a pre-specified comparison and the unconservative estimates left by unlearned failure modes
2611.03117:v1.abstract: Active-learning Kriging often replaces candidate pools by continuous metaheuristic search. A pre-specified comparison sharing surrogate, population and stopping rule isolated this inner optimizer: five budget-matched continuous optimizers, including hybrid swarm optimization with L-BFGS-B polishing, against candidate pools on eleven problems (dimension 2 to 100). The primary hypothesis was not supported: against optimizers sharing its criterion the hybrid won 6, tied 41 and lost 19 of 66 Holm-corrected accuracy comparisons, and against pool methods 0, 23 and 21 of 44. With sequential selection on three series systems, multistart L-BFGS-B left a failure mode unlearned in 59 of 60 runs, more often than swarm, genetic-algorithm or AK-MCS. In all 198 runs (22 post-freeze) with an unlearned mode, the learned modes did not compensate and failure probability was underestimated (exploratory). The error criterion can accept substantial underestimation: it accepted 17 runs (13 pool-selected) at 0.38 to 0.89 of the reference; 181 exhausted the budget. Follow-up analyses on single-design-point problems indicate underestimation when selections concentrate near the design point. Kriging-believer pool selection satisfied the surrogate stopping criterion with fewer calls than the best continuous method in all four informative batch cells (two post-freeze). We recommend default pool selection and coverage checks for any selection.

2611.03113:v1.title: Preprocessing Choices in Fine-Tuning Data Matter: Utility and Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Recommendation
2611.03113:v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced a generative approach to recommendation, producing item lists from textual representations of user histories and item information. However, this generative setting raises challenges concerning output validity, prompt consistency, and sensitivity to demographic descriptors. In this work, we investigate how preprocessing choices in fine-tuning data affect recommendation utility and fairness-related behavior in a generative LLM-based recommender system. We first establish a controlled recommendation pipeline that combines supervised fine-tuning, catalog-constrained decoding, and prompt augmentation. We then study three preprocessing choices: item-title representation, demographic balancing, and auxiliary item-knowledge enrichment. Experiments on MovieLens-1M show that the catalog-constrained pipeline eliminates out-of-catalog items and ensures complete ten-item outputs, while prompt augmentation improves prompt consistency and utility. Original MovieLens titles increase HR@10 from 10.67% to 12.47% and Coverage@10 from 41.36% to 47.88%. Fairness-related effects are attribute-dependent: age balancing and knowledge enrichment reduce selected group-level utility gaps while largely preserving utility, whereas gender balancing reduces utility without improving the evaluated gender-related indicators. Overall, preprocessing choices in fine-tuning data should be evaluated jointly in terms of utility, output behavior, and demographic sensitivity.

2610.38496:v2.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
2610.38496:v2.abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost.
