2611.00205:v1.abstract: The origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has been a long-standing mystery. A unique feature of UHECRs originating in binary neutron star mergers (BNSMs) is two distinct populations of light elements -- those directly accelerated in the jets, and photo-disintegration products of massive nuclei accelerated in the bulk outflow. We show that Pierre Auger Observatory spectrum and composition data confirm the existence of the predicted two populations at $\geq \!7.2σ$ significance, having rigidity ($R\equiv E/Ze$) cutoffs agreeing with prior estimates. The data also favor 5-10% of UHECRs originating as r-process nuclei, a signature of a BNSM origin. Our results provide strong evidence that UHECRs are produced by merging neutron stars, and show how UHECRs and UHE-neutrinos elucidate otherwise inaccessible aspects of neutron star mergers.

2611.00194:v1.title: Heavy quarkonium dynamics beyond the binding energy over temperature expansion
2611.00194:v1.abstract: We revisit the pNRQCD open-quantum-system description of bottomonium in a quark-gluon plasma, writing the full master equation in a spherical basis and establishing a framework for its numerical treatment. The equation does not rely on an expansion in the ratio of the binding energy over the temperature, while retaining the Born, Markov, and dilute approximations. It depends on suitable convolutions of Coulombic Green's functions with real-time chromoelectric correlators, rather than a finite set of transport coefficients. It contains jump-operator contributions that enter with both positive and negative signs, so it is not of a Lindblad type. We utilize optimal operator rotations to minimize the negative sector and define a positive-sector approximation that retains only the optimized positive terms, obtaining in this way a Lindblad equation that can be simulated efficiently with the open-source code QTraj for arbitrary chromoelectric spectral functions. We treat the discarded sector as a systematic uncertainty associated with positivity-breaking effects of the pseudo-Lindblad generator. Positivity breaking effects can be attributed to the approximations made in the derivation of the quarkonium master equation, such as the Born--Markov approximations. Using a spectral model constrained by known infrared and ultraviolet limits, we compute the in-medium width and Bjorken-evolved survival probabilities of the $Υ(1\mathrm{S},2\mathrm{S},3\mathrm{S})$. The computations show the convergence of the binding-energy-over-temperature expansion at high temperatures and provide the first large-scale quantum-trajectory simulation results for bottomonium in the low temperature regime. We can thus follow the bottomonium evolution over the full temperature range relevant in heavy-ion collisions.

2608.15798:v2.title: The Hardness of Estimating Cross-Entropy Risk for Language Models
2608.15798:v2.abstract: Language models, once pretrained, are routinely assessed by the holdout method, which estimates their per-token cross-entropy risk---a quantity that may be finite or infinite. We prove possibility and impossibility theorems that characterize the hardness of this estimation problem. The estimand depends on two objects: the unknown data distribution $p$ and the distribution $q$ induced by the language model under study. Our ignorance of $p$ is empirical, whereas our ignorance of $q$, or at least of its tail, is mathematical; so the parameter space {\em should} range over pairs $(p,q)$---a product space---to fully capture our ignorance. {\em Negative results}: no estimator is pointwise consistent, even when the parameter space is restricted to full-support models and to data distributions whose expected text length is below a fixed bound; worse, every estimator fails on a dense set of pairs. {\em Positive results}: the holdout estimator becomes pointwise consistent when the models are further restricted to Transformers or, architecture-neutrally, to full-support models with a finite context window; and, where no such design is in place, it still consistently estimates the risk capped at any fixed threshold, which suffices for screening candidate models in practice. {\em Lesson}: designs such as the Transformer architecture and finite context windows, although adopted for computational or engineering reasons, pay a {\em statistical dividend}: they suffice to make pointwise consistency possible---a dividend visible only in how they turn a negative result into positive ones.

2605.26315:v2.title: Curriculum Learning for Safety Alignment
2605.26315:v2.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used approach for safety alignment that aims to reduce harmful behaviors in large language models. However, prior work shows that it can be brittle and exhibits poor out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. In this paper we investigate whether Curriculum Learning can improve the robustness of DPO-based safety alignment. We propose Staged-Competence, a curriculum-based framework that organizes preference data by difficulty, employs competence-based sampling, and progressively updates the reference model during training. Averaged across three model families and three training seeds, Staged-Competence reduces OOD harmful response rates by 13.6 percentage points and attack success rates across five jailbreak attacks by 16.5 percentage points, while preserving general capabilities and maintaining near-zero over-refusal. We further show that Staged-Competence: (1) matches baseline safety performance with only 75% of the training data, demonstrating improved data efficiency and (2) yields better separation between safe and unsafe responses. Staged-Competence is agnostic to the underlying policy optimization loss and can extend to other DPO variants and alignment domains beyond safety. Additionally, we find multiple inconsistencies in standard RLHF datasets and create a cleaner combined version, named PiKacHHU. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sandeep5500/curriculum-learning-for-safety and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/etrigan5500/PiKacHHU.

2510.01824:v3.title: Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization with Order-Invariant Reinforcement Learning
2510.01824:v3.abstract: We introduce an order-invariant reinforcement learning framework for black-box combinatorial optimization. Classical estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) often rely on learning explicit variable dependency graphs, which can be costly and fail to capture complex interactions efficiently. In contrast, we parameterize a multivariate autoregressive generative model trained without a fixed variable ordering. By sampling random generation orders during training, a form of information-preserving dropout, the model is encouraged to be invariant to variable order, promoting search-space diversity, and shaping the model to focus on the most relevant variable dependencies, improving sample efficiency. We adapt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to this setting, providing stable policy-gradient updates from scale-invariant advantages. Across a wide range of benchmark algorithms and problem instances of varying sizes, our method frequently achieves the best performance and consistently avoids catastrophic failures.

2611.00187:v1.title: CAPER: Circuit-Aware Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in LLMs for Analog Verification
2611.00187:v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate analog circuits, yet every netlist must also be verified. We propose LLMs as verification assistants for analog circuits that flag unmet specifications and reliability issues that appear under process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variation. These issues emerge from how circuit stages combine, a structure that generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA do not capture. To this end, we introduce CAPER, a circuit-aware PEFT method that adds a small branch alongside LoRA to read each stage's properties from the LLM and combine them from the relevant stages. In deciding whether a feedback loop is negative, LoRA and a high-rank adapter stay at chance, whereas CAPER answers every test case correctly. For comparator latches, where 11 of 90 LLM-written designs that work under nominal conditions fail under PVT variation, CAPER likewise learns to flag such latent failures, while generic adapters stay near chance. These results show that adding circuit knowledge to PEFT makes such analog verification checks learnable through fine-tuning.

2611.00183:v1.title: The Prior-Force Family of Implicit Denoiser Priors and Its Decisions in Linear Inverse Problems
2611.00183:v1.abstract: Implicit priors given by Gaussian denoisers successfully regularize a wide range of inverse problems in approaches such as plug-and-play (PnP), regularization by denoising (RED) and score-based methods. Such a prior depends on the noise level, and how it selects among signals consistent with the data remains largely uncharacterized. To put implicit and explicit priors on the same footing, we define the prior-force family $W_t=t^{-1}(D_t^{-1}-I)$ of any Gaussian denoiser $D_t$ at noise variance $t>0$ (inverse in the graph sense), the normalized denoising residual as an operator on clean signals. At a common effective prior weight, the equilibrium equations differ only in their prior terms: PnP uses $W_t$, RED/score-based methods the score force (the normalized residual as an operator on noisy inputs), and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation the MAP force (the negative log-prior gradient). For the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) denoisers of a prior $π$, we compare the corresponding energies at three levels. Without observation, raising the noise level favors PnP minima that retain more posterior variance. On signals consistent with the data, the leading-order PnP energy for separated modes is the proximal hull of the MAP energy, which lets PnP select signals between modes; modes of equal data fit are ranked by peak height at small noise levels and by mass at large ones. For recovery, $W_t$ at the truth bounds the local bias, and an oracle noise level balances this bias against denoiser error. These results show that the noise level is a parameter of the prior rather than a step size. Experiments with exact priors support these predictions, including the mixture components that PnP selects on unseen data.

2607.10681:v2.title: Spectral Margins and Memory Routing in Looped Transformers
2607.10681:v2.abstract: Looped transformers apply one block of weights repeatedly. Each iteration keeps a fraction of the previous hidden state, the carry, and adds the block's output, so information can pass between iterations through either path. We study a small, LayerNorm-based variant of the Parcae architecture and ask two questions: does the iterated state settle, and does learning to remember across iterations require the carry? On stability, pre-LayerNorm makes the block less sensitive at its fixed point as the carry grows, but not enough to guarantee contraction: with a scalar carry, a perturbation can grow in a single iteration even at a locally stable fixed point. These fixed points are stable because the spectral radius of the loop's Jacobian stays below $1$; its distance from $1$, the spectral margin, narrows as the carry approaches $1$ and, at high carry, as the width grows, and some initializations do not settle within the iteration budget. On memory, a multi-hop copy task trained at a fixed loop depth is learned as well with the carry frozen at $0.5$, $0.02$, or $0$ as with a learned carry, which changes little during training. When the depth is sampled during training, a carry of $0.5$ still trains but $0.02$ and $0$ do not. All experiments are small ($d \le 32$ for training).

2609.40016:v2.title: Component-Weighted Centroid Search for Exact Incremental BPE
2609.40016:v2.abstract: Exact incremental tokenizers keep the tokenization of a growing text up to date, so a long prompt or agent trace is not retokenized each time it grows. Jiang and Gong's algorithm does this for byte-pair encoding (BPE) in $O(\log^2 t)$ worst-case time per byte, where $t$ is the length of the longest token. Its search passes through $O(\log t)$ nested subproblems and runs a binary search over the possible branches at each one. We weight each branch by the size of the subproblem it leads to. Each step then costs about one probe for every halving of the remaining candidates, and a whole update costs $O(\log t)$, as much as one binary search over all candidates. Output and asymptotic memory are unchanged. We also construct valid BPE vocabularies on which the original search provably needs $Θ(\log^2 t)$ probes and ours $Θ(\log t)$, and a Rust implementation reproduces both counts exactly. On six real vocabularies the two searches run at about the same speed on ordinary text, while on long runs of spaces or hyphens the weighted search is up to 2.5$\times$ faster.

2504.12971:v4.title: Transferrable Surrogates in Expressive Neural Architecture Search Spaces
2504.12971:v4.abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) faces a challenge in balancing the exploration of expressive, broad search spaces that enable architectural innovation with the need for efficient evaluation of architectures to effectively search such spaces. We investigate surrogate model training for improving search in highly expressive NAS search spaces based on context-free grammars. We show that i) surrogate models trained either using zero-cost-proxy metrics and neural graph features (GRAF) or by fine-tuning an off-the-shelf LM have high predictive power for the performance of architectures both within and across datasets, ii) these surrogates can be used to filter out bad architectures when searching on novel datasets, thereby significantly speeding up search and achieving better final performances, and iii) the surrogates can be further used directly as the search objective for huge speed-ups.

2606.08360:v2.title: Reaching Hidden Populations: Generative Frontier Planning for Peer-Referral Recruitment
2606.08360:v2.abstract: Peer-referral programs help connect populations at high risk for HIV and other infectious diseases with testing and prevention services when conventional outreach is ineffective. However, referral vouchers and incentives are limited, and standard operational guidelines give each participant the same fixed number of vouchers, ignoring differences in referral capacity. Motivated by our collaboration with public health practitioners, we study how to allocate a fixed voucher budget adaptively across participants and rounds to maximize total recruitment. Prior work assumes future recruits are i.i.d. from a population-level distribution and summarizes the recruitment frontier only by its size, ignoring covariate-dependent recruitment potential. We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), which learns referral capacity with a censored count model and referrer-conditioned recruit covariates with a conditional diffusion model. Its structured value function yields a deterministic Bellman backup shared by fitted value iteration and planning, while inducing diminishing returns that give intra-round greedy allocation a (1-1/e)-approximation guarantee for each fixed round budget. Cross-round selection then determines how much budget to spend. We evaluate GFP on two data-calibrated recruitment environments constructed from de-identified recruiter-recruit records: a public ICPSR respondent-driven sampling dataset and a dataset provided by FHI 360, an international global health nonprofit. GFP recruits up to 21.5% more individuals than the strongest baseline under the same budget, showing its potential for resource-limited peer-referral programs.

2611.00165:v1.title: Learning to bid and bundle: a posterior-sampling agent for online retail
2611.00165:v1.abstract: An online retailer launching a perishable product bids for sponsored-search clicks, discounts a bundle with an always-stocked staple and displays its remaining stock, which raises willingness to pay. It knows neither how clicks respond to its bid nor how strong and dispersed its market is, and learns both over repeated seasons from data its own decisions censor: a zero bid reveals nothing about paid clicks, and choices follow only clicks. We design a posterior-sampling agent for it. Each period it draws a market from an exact posterior and posts the bid and discount of that market's exactly solved season plan, so every action is one a fully informed seller could take. In a simulated online florist it has the lowest regret averaged over markets. In weak markets it gives up 12% to 23% of one season's revenue over 500 seasons, four to seven times less than drawing once per season. A planner acting on point estimates can stop bidding and never learn that bidding pays. The agent escapes after about three seasons on average, against fifty with one draw per season. Where displayed scarcity keeps willingness to pay above the posted price, the discount needs no learning. Customers waiting for the discount to return to its recent level look like lost sales, so frequent waiting makes the agent underrate its market. One discount per season removes waiting at a cost of 5.9% of clairvoyant revenue in a weak market and none in a strong one.

2611.00159:v1.title: A Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering Framework with Automated Cluster Cardinality Estimation Ability
2611.00159:v1.abstract: Fuzzy clustering provides a robust framework for handling ambiguous and overlapping data boundaries, yet its traditional formulation generates entirely dense membership assignments that limit noise resilience and prevent estimating the true number of clusters, when it is unknown. To address these limitations, we introduce in this paper the Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering (GSFC) framework, which incorporates a continuous sparsity penalty into the fuzzy objective function. Because closed-form solutions are precluded by the simultaneous presence of fuzzifier and sparsity exponents, we propose an efficient primal-dual bisection search coupled with specialized analytic pathways to rigorously enforce the partition constraint while organically driving trace memberships to exact zero. This mathematically enforced sparsity empowers the algorithm to autonomously estimate the true number of clusters by dynamically pruning redundant clusters, provided that it is initialized by a larger than the true number of clusters. Furthermore, we integrate a virtual noise sink to insulate outliers from the rest of the data points. The usage of the proposed framework is also extended to line segment detection. Extensive empirical evaluations across synthetic toy datasets, high-noise geometric stress tests, and real-world benchmarks (UCI wine dataset and hyperspectral images) demonstrate that GSFC effectively exceeds conventional fuzzy benchmarks while autonomously resolving cluster cardinality. Additionally, it significantly outperforms existing sparse possibilistic and probabilistic soft-clustering alternatives in line detection tasks.

2611.00157:v1.title: FlowFPR: Flow Matching Prior for Oversampled Fourier Phase Retrieval
2611.00157:v1.abstract: Fourier phase retrieval reconstructs images from magnitude measurements without phase information, but noise and channel ambiguities make natural color-image recovery challenging. Although diffusion-prior methods provide strong image constraints, their recovery can deteriorate under stronger measurement noise, and repeated generative updates incur substantial computational cost. This paper proposes FlowFPR, which integrates a pretrained Flow Matching prior with relaxed averaged alternating reflections for oversampled Fourier phase retrieval. Each outer iteration obtains a clean image estimate through a single time-dependent Flow prediction, applies measurement-consistency correction, and reconstructs the next path state after fusing the two candidates. This process requires no backpropagation of measurement errors through the Flow network. To address ineffective or excessive correction caused by prescribed fusion weights and fixed inner depths, we introduce adaptive fusion based on residual improvement and a controlled inner search combining early stopping with best-so-far candidate selection. Their combination yields a joint variant alongside the basic method and the two independent improvements. Experiments on natural face images under a common ground-truth-assisted multiple-restart evaluation protocol show that the joint variant achieves the best mean quality among the evaluated methods at the two tested nonzero noise levels, while same-hardware timing demonstrates lower end-to-end runtime than the diffusion-based baselines.

2611.00135:v1.title: Search for $\mathrm{GeV}$-scale axion-like particles in PbPb collisions
2611.00135:v1.abstract: arXiv:2611.00135v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A search is performed for the production of axion-like particles with masses in the range 3-10 GeV using PbPb collision data recorded by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $0.228~\mathrm{nb}^{-1}$ and a nucleon-nucleon centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV. This is the first search for axion-like particles produced exclusively by two photons ($\gamma\gamma\to a\to\gamma\gamma$) in the forward direction. It extends sensitivity to previously unexplored regions of the parameter space, probing axion-like particle masses and couplings down to 3.0 GeV and $3.2\times10^{-4}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$, respectively. This result provides the most stringent limits to date on the production of axion-like particles from exclusive photon-photon fusion processes with masses between 3 and 5 GeV.
authors: U. De Freitas Carneiro Da Graca

2611.00130:v1.title: FB-MOAC: A Reinforcement Learning Algorithm for Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes
2611.00130:v1.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are effective in solving problems that can be modeled as Markov decision processes (MDPs). These algorithms primarily target forward MDPs whose dynamics evolve over time from an initial state. However, several important problems in different scenarios including stochastic control and network systems exhibit both a forward and a backward dynamics. As a consequence, they cannot be expressed as a standard MDP, thereby calling for a novel theory for RL in this context. Accordingly, this work introduces the concept of Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes (FB-MDPs) for multi-objective problems, develops a novel theoretical framework to characterize their optimal solutions, and proposes a general forward-backward step-wise template that allows to adapt RL algorithms for FB-MDP problems. A Forward Backward Multi Objective Actor Critic (FB-MOAC) algorithm is introduced accordingly to obtain optimal policies with guaranteed convergence and a competitive rate with respect to standard approaches in RL. FB-MOAC is evaluated on diverse use cases in the context of mathematical finance and mobile resource management. The obtained results show that FB-MOAC outperforms the state of the art across different metrics, highlighting its ability to learn and maximize rewards.

2610.40354:v1.title: Two-peak gravitational wave spectra from supercooled two-field phase transitions
2610.40354:v1.abstract: We study the gravitational wave (GW) spectrum generated by supercooled first-order phase transitions in two-field conformal models. We construct three representative toy models that capture the essential features of these models, derive analytical criteria for the existence of two-step transitions, and show how the two-field dynamics generate a genuine two-peak GW spectrum. We identify regions of parameter space in which two-peak GW spectra are observable at LISA and the Einstein Telescope. By way of illustration, we apply our analysis to a realistic conformal dark SU(3) model.

2611.00120:v1.title: DTP-OPSD: Reinforcement Learning with Distractor-Aware Temporal-Privilege On-Policy Self-Distillation for Temporal Video Grounding
2611.00120:v1.abstract: Temporal Video Grounding (TVG) aims to localize the start and end times of an event described by a language query in a video. The task becomes particularly challenging when the same video contains multiple repeated, similar, or opposite events. On these hard examples, all responses sampled by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) may miss the target and receive zero temporal Intersection-over-Union (tIoU). Their group-relative advantages are then all zero, leaving no useful policy gradient signal. To address this, we propose DTP-OPSD, a reinforcement learning framework with distractor-aware temporal-privilege on-policy self-distillation. The student observes the clean video and generates responses on-policy, while a shared-weight teacher observes a privileged video in which the target window is marked by red full-frame borders and same-video distractor windows by blue full-frame borders. For the distillation loss, the teacher evaluates student-generated prefixes and provides dense token-level Jensen-Shannon divergence supervision. This supervision remains informative even when GRPO provides no policy gradient signal. We suppress distillation when the teacher does not outperform the student and strengthen it for groups where the teacher performs better but all student rollouts receive zero tIoU. We also construct a compact hard-interference training set through VLM screening and human verification. With only 300 additional post-training examples, DTP-OPSD achieves the highest mIoU among the compared open-source 8B models on Charades-TimeLens, ActivityNet-TimeLens, and QVHighlights-TimeLens, reaching 55.93, 54.77, and 66.71, respectively. Compared with Pure GRPO trained on the same data, DTP-OPSD improves all 12 reported metrics, with R1@0.7 gains of 1.28, 1.62, and 1.78 points on the three benchmarks. Code will be released at https://github.com/nian1125/DTP-OPSD

2611.00116:v1.title: A Scalable Two-Stage Back-End Architecture for 400GbE Data Acquisition Systems
2611.00116:v1.abstract: A primary challenge in High Energy Physics (HEP) data acquisition is the aggregation of numerous low-speed (10 Gb/s) radiation-hard data links into high-speed back-end interfaces. While high-end FPGAs traditionally perform this task, transceiver density and speed in modern devices can limit cost-effective scaling. This study proposes a two-stage architecture that utilizes mid-range FPGAs for decoding and Ethernet conversion, followed by a Microchip META-DX2+ Ethernet PHY that aggregates these streams into a 400 GbE interface. This study evaluates the design's performance, validating it as a scalable and cost-effective architecture for next-generation HEP data acquisition systems.

2611.00115:v1.title: Characterization of Next Generation Power Over Fiber Systems under Cryogenic Conditions for Advanced Physics Instrumentation
2611.00115:v1.abstract: The successful application of Power-over-Fiber (PoF) technology to power photon detection systems in DUNE prototypes operating under high-voltage and cryogenic conditions has laid the groundwork for the next generation of PoF systems operating in harsh environments. This paper presents the characterization of the main components of a new PoF system operating at 1470 and 1550 nm, including the measurement of the electrical-to-optical conversion efficiency of laser transmitters, the optical-to-electrical conversion efficiency of commercial optical power converters (OPCs), and the estimation of optical fiber attenuation under cryogenic conditions. In addition, a detailed characterization of the response of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) to light leakage from optical fibers and OPCs is presented, using 808 nm as a reference to evaluate the reduction in the SiPM response at longer wavelengths. The results of this work provide a foundation for the development of next-generation PoF systems capable of powering electronics and electrical systems for future high-energy physics experiments. In addition, the electrical isolation, low-noise operation, and long-term reliability of PoF technology could motivate its application in other research fields requiring remote power delivery under cryogenic conditions, as well as in systems where infrared photons could affect their performance.

2611.00111:v1.title: SpatialVec: A Unified Representation Learning Framework for Geospatial Objects with Boundary-Aware Sampling
2611.00111:v1.abstract: Spatial representation learning is essential for Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) applications, enabling machine learning models to capture the geometry, location, and spatial relationships of geographic entities such as points, polylines, and polygons. Existing spatial encoding methods often struggle to preserve fine-grained topological information, particularly for interactions involving complex geometries such as polylines and polygons. These approaches inadequately capture boundary structure and local spatial context, causing topology-sensitive relationships near geometry boundaries to be underrepresented in the learned embedding space. Consequently, accurately modeling complex spatial interactions remains a significant challenge for downstream spatial reasoning tasks. To fill the gap, we introduce SpatialVec, a boundary-aware spatial representation learning framework that adaptively samples geometry boundaries and their surrounding regions, capturing fine-grained geometric structures critical for topology-aware spatial reasoning. A transformer-based encoder-decoder trained through geometry reconstruction produces compact, geometry-aware, and unified representations for points, polylines, and polygons. Empirical evaluation on two real-world datasets shows that SpatialVec substantially improves the preservation of challenging topological relationships involving polygonal interactions and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines significantly on downstream prediction and classification tasks.

2611.00108:v1.title: Inverse modelling of a laser-plasma accelerator
2611.00108:v1.abstract: The electron beams of a laser-plasma accelerator depend non-linearly on the laser and gas settings. This dependence is explored using particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations, and machine-learning models trained on these simulations predict the beam from the settings. Here we address the reverse problem: given a measured beam, which settings produced it? We infer three of them: the gas pressure $p\_1$, the normalised vector potential $a\_0$ and the nitrogen concentration $c\_{N\_2}$. The solution is not guaranteed to be unique. We train an ensemble of mixture density networks that, for each beam, output several possible sets of settings with their probabilities and uncertainties, and test them on simulated beams with realistic measurement noise. On average, the predictions are accurate ($R^2 = 0.91$), yet for about two-thirds of the beams the inferred distribution has two competing solutions. These share nearly the same value of $a\_0^2 p\_1$, which controls how strongly the laser focuses itself in the plasma and, in earlier PALLAS studies, when electrons start to be injected. Keeping this quantity fixed gives beams that are practically indistinguishable with realistic diagnostics. A forward model used as a check removes unphysical solutions but cannot choose between the two plausible ones. We then test two ways to resolve the ambiguity. Adding the full electron energy spectrum improves the mean prediction ($R^2 = 0.94$), mostly through $a\_0$. It changes the weights of the two solutions but does not move them. A second measurement at a deliberately different plasma density is more effective. In paired PIC simulations, it reduces the error on $a\_0$ by a factor of 2.6, whereas repeating the measurement at the same density brings almost no gain.

2611.00107:v1.title: Dynamic Merging Mutually-Distilled Multi-View Networks for RGB-Event-based Representation Learning
2611.00107:v1.abstract: arXiv:2611.00107v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-modal fusion algorithms combining conventional frame-based cameras and event cameras have recently attracted substantial research attention. Typically, existing approaches convert event streams into frames, voxels, or tensors, and then learn the required spatiotemporal information from these transformed event representations for fusion with conventional frame-camera data. Obviously, such paradigms only exploit the limited representational capacity of event data. Moreover, standard training pipelines fail to fully leverage diverse model parameters obtained throughout the learning process. In this paper, we propose a novel mutual distillation method leveraging multi-view teacher network weights to better integrate multiple event representations and achieve model-parameter level fusion. Specifically, we employ multiple encoders to extract different types of event representations and perform mutual knowledge distillation at both the feature-level and logit-level in this process. Afterwards, we perform a dynamic hierarchical model merge strategy on the model parameters from the first stage to yield a unified multi-modal RGB-Event representation model. Experimental results across multiple event-based datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves significant performance improvements.

2611.00104:v1.title: SpikePID: Real-Time Neuromorphic Cluster Counting in Future Drift Chambers
2611.00104:v1.abstract: Cluster counting ($dN/dx$) measures discrete ionization occurrences along a charged particle track traversing a gaseous medium and is currently being proposed to serve particle identification (PID) in next-generation drift chambers, as it is expected to offer higher separation power than the traditional approach based on the ionization energy loss measurement ($dE/dx$), which has intrinsically larger statistical fluctuations. However, measuring $dN/dx$ in drift chambers proposed for future colliders requires high-resolution waveforms, which result in very large data rates. Running the reconstruction at the edge would drastically reduce the bandwidth required to transmit data off the detector. In this paper, we introduce SpikePID, a neuromorphic computing approach applying spiking neural networks (SNNs) to this task due to their inherently sparse computing and processing nature. We show that an SNN with only 529 parameters improves the kaon-pion separation power by 17% over the traditional derivative-based method and by 4% over an MLP that has $8.6\times$ more parameters. When synthesized to an FPGA, it uses an order of magnitude fewer resources than the MLP, and has an inference latency compatible with the constraints of future collider experiments, making the SNN an excellent algorithmic candidate for real-time data readout in future drift chambers.

2611.00103:v1.title: Causal Multiscale Modeling of Ocular FLASH Electroretinography: Model Development, Experimental Fitting, and Spin-Glass--Percolation Predictions
2611.00103:v1.abstract: Purpose: To develop a causal multiscale model of retinal electroretinography (ERG) after ocular ultrahigh-dose-rate (FLASH) and conventional-dose-rate (CONV) irradiation, evaluate the framework against published ocular ERG data, and derive prospective dose-response predictions for future validation. Methods: The retina was coarse-grained into $N=200$ functional modules. Local rate equations were formulated as Hodgkin--Huxley-inspired conductance-balance/RC reductions of retinal ion-channel and synaptic pathways. Radiation generated an injury field that altered phototransduction, a-wave and b-wave dynamics and, in the network extension, inter-module coupling and bond survival. A reduced amplitude benchmark and nested M0/M1/M2 causal models were evaluated. Results: The reduced benchmark achieved $R^2=0.9721$ and RMSE $=11.94~μ$V. M0, M1, and M2 yielded $R^2=0.8546$, 0.8559, and 0.8560, respectively, indicating limited independent identifiability of the network terms from amplitude data alone. Under an exploratory 50\% retained-gain criterion, the reduced benchmark predicted a-wave preservation thresholds of 28.6 Gy for FLASH and 23.7 Gy for CONV, and b-wave thresholds of 29.2 Gy and 24.1 Gy, respectively, corresponding to a model-based functional dose-modifying factor (DMF) of 1.21. Conclusion: The ERG amplitude data support the causal radiation-injury-to-ERG framework, while additional observables will be needed to distinguish the predicted collective-network contributions. The model also provides quantitative dose targets for prospective studies of the FLASH retinal-preservation window and a framework for testing how local retinal injury may propagate into collective dysfunction.

arxiv:2611.00930.title: From Kination to Detection: Scotogenic Scalar Dark Matter
arxiv:2611.00930.abstract: We investigate scalar dark matter in the scotogenic model during an early kination-dominated epoch. The enhanced expansion rate causes earlier freeze-out and increases the relic abundance, opening viable dark matter masses from approximately $200~\mathrm{GeV}$ to $1~\mathrm{TeV}$ while reducing the need for co-annihilation with a nearly degenerate singlet fermion. Current indirect searches strongly constrain the $(100-200)~\mathrm{GeV}$ region, whereas much of the surviving parameter space can be probed by CTA and next-generation direct detection experiments. The viable spectra also lead to complementary collider signatures, including missing transverse energy, displaced leptons, and disappearing charged tracks, providing promising tests at the HL-LHC and future lepton colliders.

arxiv:2611.01228.title: Cuscuton Fifth Force: Implications of Non-Dynamical Scalars for Structure Growth
arxiv:2611.01228.abstract: The cuscuton is a scalar field that obeys a constraint rather than an evolution equation, so it modifies gravity without adding a propagating scalar degree of freedom. We study the cosmology of effective cuscuton theory when matter is minimally coupled in the Jordan frame, and therefore conformally coupled to the cuscuton in the Einstein-frame. We derive the background and linear perturbation equations and show that the algebraic cuscuton response mediates a fifth force even though the scalar itself does not propagate. The same conformal factor also changes Einstein-frame particle masses and the friction of matter perturbations, tying the strength and sign of the force to the background evolution rather than to an independent coupling. We study a power-law family of models which contain both tracking solutions and sign-switching solutions; in the latter the effective cuscuton density runs from negative during matter domination to a positive, cosmological-constant-like value today. Using a modified version of CLASS, including the induced particle-mass dependence of recombination, we illustrate the corresponding changes to CMB temperature and linear matter power spectra for benchmark models, without fitting to data. In the strongest benchmarks the fifth force changes the effective gravitational coupling on sub-horizon scales by about one percent, smaller than the accompanying changes to the matter power spectrum and the acoustic scale. For the sign-switching solutions this change is negative over most of cosmic history, so a non-propagating field can weaken rather than strengthen gravitational attraction.

arxiv:2610.39740.title: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) - System Design and Instrumentation
arxiv:2610.39740.abstract: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is designed to measure cosmic neutrinos in the EeV range through an array of radio antennas detecting nanosecond-long radio flashes. In this contribution, the RNO-G electronic system is outlined, illustrating how signals are measured from the antennas to the recorded pulses. We present new instrumentation developments, focusing on electric melters to install LPDA antennas into the Greenlandic ice sheet. The new system will simplify deployment and reduce positioning uncertainty to $\pm$2cm (x/y) and $\pm$1°(rotational). We report on field tests from the RNO-G site at Summit Station.

arxiv:2610.35379.title: Revisiting supernova constraints on dark gauge bosons
arxiv:2610.35379.abstract: We revisit the supernova constraints on three well-motivated light gauge bosons: the dark photon, the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson, and the $U(1)_{L_μ-L_τ}$ gauge boson. For the dark photon and the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson, we re-evaluate the nucleon bremsstrahlung process within the one-pion exchange approximation, retaining the full momentum and mass dependence. The geometrical dependence of the decay and absorption of these gauge bosons inside the supernova core is also taken into account. Updated bounds on these models are derived based on the cooling of SN1987A and energy deposition constraints from low-energy supernovae (LESNe). Taking the SFHo-18.8 $18.8\,M_\odot$ profile, the SN1987A cooling constraints reach masses of about $230$ MeV, $280$ MeV, and $300$ MeV for the dark photon, the $U(1)_{B-L}$ boson, and the $U(1)_{L_μ-L_τ}$ boson, while the corresponding LESN limits extend to about $450$ MeV, $440$ MeV, and $600$ MeV, respectively. The kinetic mixing parameter $ε$ for dark photon, the gauge coupling $g_{BL}$ in the $U(1)_{B-L}$ model, and the gauge coupling $g_{μτ}$ for the $U(1)_{L_μ-L_τ}$ model are constrained down to $5.8\times10^{-12}$, $2.9\times10^{-16}$, and $6.4\times10^{-12}$, respectively.

arxiv:2610.36161.title: Asymmetric Reheating of a Dark Sector
arxiv:2610.36161.abstract: We study asymmetric post-inflationary reheating in a framework with two sequestered MSSM-like sectors (the ``visible'' and ``dark'' sectors) with different supersymmetry-breaking scales, with dark matter corresponding to the lightest dark baryons. In this setup, independent Affleck-Dine dynamics in the two sectors offers a natural explanation for the comparable abundances of visible and dark matter. We relate the resulting temperature hierarchy to the inflaton's partial decay widths in different kinematical regimes, where it may decay into dark sector particles via 2-, 3- or 4-body processes. The latter case yields the most asymmetric reheating scenario, and we discuss the implications of this regime for the dark sector's thermal history, namely regarding the corresponding strong and weak interactions. While in this kinematical regime the contribution of light dark sector degrees of freedom to $ΔN_{\rm eff}$ is negligible, we show that it increases significantly in the regime where 3-body decays are possible, particularly near the threshold for dark Higgs pair-production where $ΔN_{\rm eff}^{\max} \simeq 0.078$. The current combined BBN+CMB+BAO bound leaves only a narrow allowed interval of the 2-body decay regime immediately above threshold, while next-generation CMB experiments could probe slightly below it.

arxiv:2610.36074.title: CROMA: a GPU-accelerated Fokker--Planck solver for modeling non-thermal emission in post-processing cosmological simulations
arxiv:2610.36074.abstract: Numerical modeling of cosmic-ray (CR) spectra and the resulting non-thermal emission is important for understanding the physical mechanisms of CR acceleration and transport in astrophysical environments. Galaxy clusters and cosmic filaments provide particularly important environments for studying these processes, where shocks, turbulence, magnetic fields, and CRs jointly shape diffuse synchrotron emission. Spectrally resolved modeling of CRs, including cooling, re-acceleration, and hadronic interactions, requires solving time-dependent Fokker--Planck (FP) equations. An increasing number of studies employ FP solvers coupled with magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations to follow the evolution of CRs in dynamically evolving environments. We present a new C/C++-based FP solver with GPU acceleration for post-processing outputs from cosmological MHD simulations. The code evolves CR proton and electron spectra along Lagrangian tracer trajectories and consistently includes re-acceleration and secondary-particle production processes. With the Chang--Cooper finite-difference scheme, the FP equation for each tracer is reduced to an independent tridiagonal system, which is solved on NVIDIA GPUs using a CUDA implementation of the parallel cyclic reduction (PCR) algorithm. The code uses sub-stepping between tracer snapshots, with the timestep constrained by the relevant CR cooling or re-acceleration timescale, and a batching algorithm that groups tracers with similar sub-stepping patterns for efficient execution. We find that the GPU acceleration increases the per-node throughput by a factor of $\approx$10 on the Leonardo Booster system operated by CINECA. The fast FP solver is useful for high-resolution simulations dedicated to comparison with next-generation radio observations and future multi-messenger applications combining radio, gamma-ray, and high-energy neutrino observations.

arxiv:2610.36282.title: Reconstruction of very inclined air showers with radio data and application to the first GRANDProto300 cosmic-ray candidates
arxiv:2610.36282.abstract: Radio detection of very inclined extensive air showers (EAS) offers a promising way to study ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and neutrinos above $10^{17}$ eV. We present a method to reconstruct the arrival direction and energy of EAS with zenith angles above $60^\circ$, applicable in principle to upward-going neutrino-induced showers. The approach combines a point-source-like description of the radio wavefront with the Angular Distribution Function (ADF), a phenomenological model describing the angular pattern of electric field amplitudes in the 50-200 MHz band. On realistic cosmic-ray simulations, we achieve better than $0.07^\circ$ resolution on arrival direction and ~15% on primary energy. Applied directly to voltage traces, this method allows efficient cosmic-ray selection with accurate direction reconstruction and first-order energy estimation. We illustrate the method on the first cosmic-ray candidates detected by the GRANDProto300 prototype of GRAND, validating its detection principle and paving the way for high-precision neutrino searches.

doi:10.1140/epjh/s13129-026-00138-w.title: Double $\beta$-decay: unveiling the early history of a rare process
doi:10.1140/epjh/s13129-026-00138-w.abstract: Neutrinos are currently the subject of intensive theoretical and experimental investigations, devoted to looking for new evidence of physics beyond the Standard Model of elementary particles. The solution of puzzling issues such as the mass-generation mechanism, the lepton number violation, the absolute mass scale and the possible Majorana nature of neutrinos would open also new perspectives on baryogenesis and the evolution of the universe. In this respect, the observation of the rarest and elusive neutrinoless double $\beta $-decay process is expected to play a prominent role, so that its relevance can be hardly underestimated. In the present work, we fully reconstruct the genesis and the early history of double $\beta $-decay, starting from Maria Goeppert-Mayer's pioneering contribution, which promptly followed the first successful theory of $\beta $-decay provided by Enrico Fermi. Furthermore, we delve into Ettore Majorana's neutrino theory and a variety of related investigations, finally focusing on the neutrinoless version of double $\beta $-decay, whose existence was suggested by Wendell H. Furry in 1939 and put forward as a viable tool to discriminate between the very (Dirac or Majorana) nature of the electron neutrino.

arxiv:2610.33879.title: Finite-temperature ab-initio-Informed Nuclear Equation-of-State Tables (FINEST): Nuclear matter uncertainties in core-collapse supernovae
arxiv:2610.33879.abstract: We construct new finite-temperature, composition-dependent equation of state (EOS) tables for astrophysical simulations by implementing a recently developed energy-density functional. The functional is constrained by ab initio nuclear matter calculations and neutron-star observations. A distinguishing feature of this functional is a non-monotonic density dependence of the nucleon effective mass, with an increase beyond saturation density. Using these EOS tables, we investigate the impact of current uncertainties in nuclear matter properties on core-collapse supernova (CCSN) evolution with spherically symmetric simulations employing an effective treatment of convective mixing. The magnitude of the EOS effects depends on the progenitor compactness. Within current constraints, variations in incompressibility, symmetry energy, and high-density pressure produce only modest differences during the early post-bounce evolution. In contrast, the effective mass dependence has a much stronger influence on proto-neutron star contraction and the explosion dynamics in a stellar model with high core compactness. Its non-monotonic density dependence leads to a qualitatively different contraction history and can alter the explosion outcome compared to mean-field effective-mass behaviors. Therefore, among the nuclear matter properties considered, the density dependence of the nucleon effective masses has by far the largest impact on CCSN dynamics. This highlights the importance of realistic effective-mass parameterizations in nuclear EOSs used in astrophysical simulations.

arxiv:2610.33954.title: Core-Collapse Supernovae from Single and Binary-Stripped Massive Stars - I. Explodability and Nucleosynthesis
arxiv:2610.33954.abstract: Binary interaction can substantially alter massive-star evolution and pre-supernova structure, changing core-collapse outcomes and nucleosynthetic yields. We compare explodability and nucleosynthesis in 66 non-rotating, solar-metallicity single-star and binary-stripped progenitors spanning zero-age main-sequence (ZAMS) masses of $11$-$45\,{\rm M}_\odot$, using the spherically symmetric PUSH framework and nucleosynthesis post-processing. Both populations explode up to $22\,{\rm M}_\odot$, with binary stripping altering explodability at higher ZAMS masses. Successful explosions span similar energies ($\sim$0.4-1.3$\,$B) and remnant masses ($\sim$1.4-2.0$\,{\rm M}_\odot$). The largest nucleosynthetic differences occur at low ZAMS masses, particularly for material undergoing explosive O and Si burning. The $^{56}$Ni yields and iron-group abundances broadly agree with observations of core-collapse supernovae and the metal-poor star HD 84937. When compared with calculations using time-dependent mixing-length theory and a two-parameter explodability criterion for the same progenitors, our results reveal substantial differences in explodability, with agreement on successful explosions for only 5 cases across all three approaches. Nevertheless, elemental yield patterns can remain broadly similar for models that explode successfully across treatments. Salpeter initial-mass-function-weighted yields of most elements differ by $\sim$20% between populations, with K enhanced by a factor of $\sim$3.4 in the binary-stripped population, driven by increased production in the lowest-mass progenitors. Binary-stripped models show closer agreement with empirical core-collapse S, K, and Ca abundance ratios relative to Mg inferred from APOGEE, while Na remains overproduced in both populations. Together, our results highlight the need to account for binarity when interpreting supernova abundance patterns.

arxiv:2610.32619.title: Development of an Analog Front-End Using NINO ASIC for Mini-ICAL
arxiv:2610.32619.abstract: The mini-ICAL was supposed to be a pre-prototype detector of the Iron CALorimeter (ICAL) of the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) project. Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) was the active element of these detectors. As this detector operates in avalanche mode, one needs a very fast pre-amplifier for signal processing. NINO ASIC developed for the ALICE time-of-flight detector was a potential chip to be used as the analog-front end. This paper presents an 8-in-1 pre-amplifier board developed using the NINO ASIC, a single-ended to differential signal conversion using the differential driver chip manufactured by Texas Instruments, production of the boards, lessons learned during production, testing of these boards, and interface with RPCs. Finally, its performance based on strip rates and efficiency of the detector will also be discussed.

arxiv:2610.35945.title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
arxiv:2610.35945.abstract: SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy. To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $μ$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

arxiv:2610.31755.title: From Inspiral to Outburst: Modeling a Potential Luminous Red Nova from Betelgeuse
arxiv:2610.31755.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that Betelgeuse may host a stellar companion whose orbit will decay through tidal interactions, ultimately leading to engulfment and merger within the next several thousand years. If confirmed, this system could represent the nearest and best-characterized progenitor of a future luminous red nova (LRN). We investigate whether the shock-breakout and cooling emission preceding the LRN can be used to constrain the properties of the companion and its disruption within the stellar envelope. Using binary stellar evolution calculations, we evolve Betelgeuse with companions of $0.7$, $1.0$, and $2.0 M_\odot$ to the onset of common envelope evolution (CEE). We then perform one-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulations that follow companion disruption, energy deposition, and shock propagation through the envelope. We find that the peak luminosity increases systematically with companion mass, from $2.44\times10^{41}$ to $6.17\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ across the $0.7$-$2.0 M_\odot$ models, while the duration increases more modestly from $1.48$ to $1.99$ days and attains apparent magnitudes brighter than Venus as viewed from Earth. Tidal disruption contributes both kinetic energy and mass to the envelope, linking the companion's structure and mass to the energetics of the shock-heated ejecta. The monotonic luminosity sequence demonstrates that the early breakout emission can retain direct information about the engulfed companion. The interaction ejects $6.15$-$11.19 M_\odot$ of hydrogen-rich material, substantially modifying both the envelope structure and circumstellar environment prior to core collapse.

arxiv:2610.31758.title: Collapsars Are Not Heavy $r$-Process Factories
arxiv:2610.31758.abstract: Collapsar disks are proposed sources of $r$-process elements, but neutron-rich disk ejecta require gas to be both neutronized in the disk and ejected before accretion. The magnetic field that enables ejection also thickens the disk and accelerates the inflow, lowering both the density and the time available for weak processing. To compute the resulting neutronization, we evolve the electron fraction of the inflowing gas, adopting at each radius the temperature that maximizes the net neutronization rate for the local density and instantaneous composition. This yields a lower limit on $Y_{\rm e}$ that is independent of the disk's thermal history. We adopt an optimistic unbinding radius of $R_{\rm unb}=10\,r_g$ for all magnetic fluxes capable of launching outflows. Combining this ejection condition with favorable assumptions of low black hole mass, ejection of midplane gas, and the upper end of the $γ$-ray burst (GRB) engine-power scale, which limits the accretion rate to $\dot M_{\rm BH}\lesssim0.4\,M_\odot\,{\rm s}^{-1}$, gives a fiducial lower bound $Y_{\rm e}\gtrsim0.33$, above the characteristic $Y_{\rm e}\approx 0.25$ threshold for heavy $r$-process production. Stronger magnetic flux, toward which jet-launching engines evolve, raises the lower bound to $Y_{\rm e}\gtrsim0.49$. We conclude that collapsar disk outflows cannot supply the heavy $r$-process yields invoked for a dominant enrichment channel. Only engines with unusually high accretion rates, potentially including exceptionally luminous GRBs, such as GRB 221009A, and direct-horizon collapsars, may produce heavy $r$-process ejecta.

arxiv:2610.30240.title: Probing Heavy Neutral Leptons through New Gauge Interactions at the Forward Physics Facilities
arxiv:2610.30240.abstract: We investigate the prospects for improving the heavy neutral lepton (HNL) searches at the far-forward LHC experiments FASER and FASER$ν$, as well as their proposed HL-LHC successors, FASER2 and FASER$ν$2, using new HNL production mechanisms. We consider scenarios in which HNLs couple directly to a new $U(1)$ gauge boson and decay into visible Standard Model final states through mixing with active neutrinos. Focusing on the $U(1)_{B-L}$, $U(1)_{B-3L_τ}$, and $U(1)_B$ gauge extensions as benchmark models, we study HNL production through proton bremsstrahlung and Drell--Yan processes, which probe complementary mediator-mass regimes. We analyze several visible decay channels, including charged leptons, neutral mesons, and other hadrons, and evaluate the projected sensitivities for different neutrino-flavor mixing patterns. We find that these new production mechanisms that differ qualitatively from the conventional picture in which both production and decay are controlled by active-sterile mixing enable the far-forward LHC program to probe previously unexplored regions of HNL parameter space, with the first-ever demonstration of FASER$ν$ having sensitivity to HNLs and FASER2 and FASER$ν$2 offering substantially enhanced sensitivity during the HL-LHC era, even reaching the canonical seesaw prediction for all three lepton flavors. Our results demonstrate that new gauge interactions can substantially enhance HNL production independently of the active-sterile mixing that governs their visible decays, opening complementary opportunities to explore HNLs at the forward physics facilities.

doi:10.1007/s41365-026-02048-4.title: Rejection of pile-up events in Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillating bolometers for neutrinoless double-beta decay detection
doi:10.1007/s41365-026-02048-4.abstract:
Neutrinoless double-beta decay (0$
u  eta  eta$) detection necessitates an exceptionally low background, as this hypothesized process has not been observed; current experimental lower limits on its half-life are of order $10^{26}$ years. When the intrinsic background from the detector and its passive support materials is low, the primary sources of this background in 0$
u  eta  eta$ experiments of $^{100}$Mo are the pile-up events of two-neutrino double-beta decay events and alpha events. This work presents methods that contribute to further reducing pile-up events, thereby supporting the feasibility of 0$
u  eta  eta$ detection. One is a time-over-threshold (TOT) method, wherein the amplitude of the signal is compared against a threshold, and the duration of the signal exceeding the threshold is measured. This method aims to discern pile-up events by analyzing the time duration discrepancy between pile-up events and single events of equivalent amplitude. Using MATLAB, the double-exponential ideal waveform is first generated, followed by the addition of white Gaussian noise to simulate realistic signal conditions. The method is evaluated in two scenarios: a constant threshold and a dynamically changing threshold. Compared with a constant threshold, a dynamic threshold that adjusts according to the waveform can effectively improve discrimination efficiency. The results demonstrate that the TOT method with a dynamically changing threshold reaches a discrimination efficiency of 92.5% at a signal-to-noise ratio of 30, and that at higher signal-to-noise ratios its efficiency is comparable to that of the traditional mean-time method. This paper also attempts to improve the mean-time method, including the generalization of the mean-time definition and its combination with the TOT method. Moreover, in this paper, calculations of the achievable background index for projected light detectors under different rise times and signal-to-noise ratios are performed. In an actual experiment, the background index is influenced by various factors beyond the simulation work. Nevertheless, the background suppression scheme proposed in this work provides a solid foundation for the next-generation CUPID experiment to achieve the physics goal, reducing the background index below $1	imes 10^{-4}$ counts/(keV$\cdot$kg$\cdot$yr).

arxiv:2610.28482.title: The "Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery" Workshop: A Community Roadmap for the Future of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory After the LSST
arxiv:2610.28482.abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory will complete its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in the mid-2030s. Its 8.4 m aperture and 9.6 square degree field of view give it an étendue unmatched by any facility planned for that era. The Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop (KIPAC/SLAC, 3-5 August 2026) brought together approximately 100 participants to discuss Rubin's future after LSST. This paper summarizes the workshop's structure and discussions across five working groups. The continued-surveying group explored a machine-learning foundation model pretrained on Rubin imaging for detection, deblending, and classification. The cadence group considered allocating post-LSST observing time and strategies for transiting exoplanets, Type Ia supernova cosmology, time-delay cosmography, and second-scale transients. The filter group explored broadband, medium-band, and narrowband filters for photometric redshifts, high-redshift large-scale structure, AGN reverberation mapping, Galactic archaeology, and emission-line imaging. The multi-messenger group explored follow-up of next-generation gravitational-wave and neutrino sources, including standard sirens, kilonovae, and Galactic supernovae. The technology group organized options by cost and lead time, including fast readout, new filters, a faster shutter, and summit edge computing. Cross-cutting topics included AI/ML, Chilean and Latin-American co-leadership, satellite megaconstellations, and weather and climate trends at Cerro Pachón. White papers and workshop talks are available through https://zenodo.org/communities/rubin2036workshop/ and https://rubin-observatory.github.io/Rubin-Beyond-LSST/pages/Rubin2036proceedings/.

doi:10.1134/s1062873826701893.title: Baksan Large Neutrino Telescope: Project Development and Infrastructure Design
doi:10.1134/s1062873826701893.abstract: The current status of the Baksan Large Neutrino Telescope project is presented in this work. The results of the first stage-a prototype with a target mass of 0.5 t-were described. The main improvements in the second prototype were also outlined: the magnetic field compensation system and the liquid scintillator purification system.

doi:10.1134/s1062873826701881.title: Multipurpose Compact Neutrino Detector Based on a Gadolinium-Gallium-Containing Scintillator
doi:10.1134/s1062873826701881.abstract: A concept of a multipurpose compact neutrino detector based on GAGG:Ce crystals is proposed. Its potential applications include testing the gallium anomaly using artificial neutrino sources, searching for 2νββ and 0νββ decays of the $^{160}$Gd isotope, as well as detecting solar neutrinos. A prototype of a unit cell for such a detector is presented.

doi:10.1007/s10751-026-02800-7.title: Energy loss and quenching-factor studies for low-recoil collision cascades in silicon using molecular dynamics simulations
doi:10.1007/s10751-026-02800-7.abstract: Low-energy nuclear recoils in semiconductor detectors like Silicon (Si) and Germanium (Ge), play a crucial role in direct Dark-Matter detection and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$\nu$NS) experiments. In this preliminary work, we employ classical molecular dynamics simulations to investigate energy-partitioning processes in crystalline silicon for recoil energies ranging from 20 eV to 10 keV. Silicon primary knock-on atoms (PKAs) were initiated within a $(20 \times 20 \times 20)\,\text { \text{\AA }}^{3}$ Silicon supercell using periodic diamond-cubic lattice, and the resulting collision cascades were analyzed using molecular dynamics framework together with an energy-dependent electronic stopping derived from SRIM calculations. The partitioning of recoil energy between atomic motion and electronic energy dissipation was quantified, and quenching factors (QFs) were estimated from the cumulative electronic energy loss. The calculated QF values exhibit systematic deviations from the Lindhard's model in the sub-10 keV regime, indicating a reduced electronic-energy fraction for low-energy recoils. Comparison with available experimental data shows overall qualitative agreement across the investigated energy range. The preliminary results of this study demonstrate the potential of atomistic molecular dynamics simulations to provide microscopic insight into low-energy recoil processes and detector response in silicon-based rare-event searches. Further simulations, analysis and studies are going on to get much deeper understanding of the findings.

doi:10.1103/kjkf-x79r.title: Neutrino flux from collisions of red giant cores in globular clusters
doi:10.1103/kjkf-x79r.abstract: The coalescence of degenerate helium cores during red giant collisions—a process we term “erythrohenosis”—introduces a novel class of transient astrophysical sources of high-energy neutrinos. Using stellar models generated with mesa and smoothed-particle hydrodynamics simulations of the final inspiral phase, we develop a semianalytical model to estimate the amount of hydrogen mixed into the cores, the energy release ( ≈ 4.28 × 10 49 erg ) that heats the remnant to T f ≈ 5.3 × 10 8 K , the magnetic field amplification ( B ≈ 1.77 × 10 10 G ), and the resulting neutrino flux. The predicted TeV–PeV neutrino signal may contribute to the diffuse IceCube neutrino flux; we estimate that the horizon at which a single neutrino event is expected on average at ≳ 100 TeV is ≈ 55 kpc for individual merger events. Furthermore, we discuss the probability of a magnetized helium flash and assess the subsequent activation of the CNO cycle in the remnant core due to hydrogen mixing. In particular, neutrinos from the decay of F 18 offer a direct observational test of the detonation, (as sources within ∼ 4.4 pc would produce a neutrino flux exceeding the solar CNO neutrino background). The simultaneous emission of high-energy hadronic neutrinos, gravitational waves, and—if the optical depth permits ( τ T ∼ 10 14 in the core of the remnant)—an electromagnetic signal would constitute a unique multimessenger signature of red giant core collisions, positioning erythrohenosis events as exotic yet potentially observable phenomena in dense stellar systems.

arxiv:2610.16968.title: Self-Interacting Dark Matter: From Particle Physics Theories to Structure Formation Simulations
arxiv:2610.16968.abstract: We establish a unified theory-to-simulation framework for self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) that integrates three components: (i) a comprehensive, self-contained treatment of its particle-physics foundations and a broad range of model classes; (ii) a systematic, quantitative mapping from microscopic dark-sector physics to structure-formation simulation inputs through explicit expressions and numerical prescriptions; and (iii) the development, implementation, and validation of a broad suite of SIDM algorithms and a dedicated DM decay module in the moving-mesh code AREPO-2. Under (i), we detail the particle content, symmetries, interactions, production mechanisms, and constraints of a broad landscape of elementary and composite SIDM models, and present representative viable benchmark models. Under (ii), the mapping specifies cosmological initial conditions, internal-state masses and populations, reaction networks, velocity- and angle-dependent cross sections, dissipative energy loss, and decay rates and recoil kinematics. We then apply this mapping to a broad range of SIDM model classes. Under (iii), we implement and validate SIDM algorithms with constant and velocity-dependent cross sections, covering isotropic and anisotropic scattering, multi-state elastic and inelastic reactions, and dissipative processes, alongside a dedicated DM decay module in AREPO-2. We validate these implementations through beam-lattice deflection experiments, thermalization and uniform-box decay tests, isolated-halo gravothermal core-collapse simulations, and cosmological box and zoom-in simulations. These tests recover analytical predictions, establish agreement across numerical schemes, and reproduce published benchmarks. Our theory-to-simulation framework serves as a cross-disciplinary reference and a practical bridge between SIDM particle physics and simulations of nonlinear structure formation.

arxiv:2610.14178.title: Collider and direct detection as key probes of asymmetric dark matter: Signals from a compressed Inert Higgs doublet
arxiv:2610.14178.abstract: The cosmic imbalance of particles over antiparticles may be inherited by the dark matter in a certain class of asymmetric dark matter models. In this article, we thoroughly investigate the signatures of the minimal realization of this idea. In this model a new (stable) inert Higgs, $H'$, plays the role of the mediator that facilitates the asymmetry transfer from the visible to the dark sector. It also constitutes a small dark matter sub-component, while the dominant component stems from a singlet scalar asymmetry. A combination of phenomenological and cosmological constraints requires this new inert Higgs doublet to be quite light $46\,{\rm GeV}<m_{H'}< 580\,{\rm GeV}$ and its spectrum rather compressed, $ΔM = m_{H^\pm}-m_{H_0} \lesssim 1\,{\rm GeV}$ and $δm = m_{A_0}-m_{H_0}\lesssim 5\,{\rm MeV}$. Therefore its charged component can be relatively long-lived on collider length-scales. By recasting searches for compressed Higgsinos at the LHC, we derive new limits on this particle and show that, while at present most of the parameter space for this state is still unconstrained, large and key regions of parameter space will be tested at the HL-LHC by a combination of searches for disappearing charged tracks and displaced soft tracks. Quite remarkably, the lifetime of the charged component of the doublet can be correlated with the dark matter interaction rate at direct detection experiments and we show that the next generation of direct detection experiments has a unique sensitivity to the parameter space in the model. The fact that a small neutral mass splitting is a prediction of the asymmetric setup makes it an interesting candidate to account for the high energy nuclear recoil event recently reported by the LZ experiment. More generally, our detailed phenomenological study holds for any dark matter model involving an inert Higgs doublet with mass below 580 GeV.

arxiv:2610.11839.title: Searching for Charged Lepton Flavor Violation
arxiv:2610.11839.abstract: Searches for Charged Lepton Flavor Violation (CLFV) are powerful tools to probe physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). This chapter provides a comprehensive survey of CLFV theory, focusing primarily on low-energy muon and tau transitions while outlining complementary searches from high-energy colliders. Grounded in the Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework, we systematically review key observables including radiative and purely leptonic decays of muon and tau as well as $μ\to e$ conversion in nuclei and $τ$ hadronic decay channels. CLFV involving light new physics particles is also discussed. This review captures the modern synergy between EFTs, novel light-mediator scenarios, and hadronic and nuclear physics in the ongoing hunt for BSM signals.

arxiv:2609.20552.title: Mineral Detection of Neutrinos and Dark Matter 2026 Proceedings
arxiv:2609.20552.abstract: The fourth "Mineral Detection of Neutrinos and Dark Matter" (MDvDM'26) meeting was held April 14-17, 2026 in Karlsruhe, Germany, hosted by the Institute for Astroparticle Physics (IAP) at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT). These proceedings detail the contributions that were presented during MDvDM'26, illustrating the unprecedented progress in theoretical, computational and experimental studies towards the realization of the concept of mineral detectors. Mineral detectors represent an emerging particle detection concept that has risen in prominence in recent years due to the advent of modern computational and high-resolution microscopy techniques. Natural and synthetic crystals are capable of retaining microscopic damage features induced by nuclear recoils, which could be then read out with a variety of micrometer and nanometer resolution microscopy techniques. On laboratory time scales mineral detectors could be employed for reactor neutrino monitoring and dark matter detection, with the potential to measure the directions as well as the energies of the induced nuclear recoils. Uniquely, ancient natural crystals (so-called paleo-detectors) that have been recording nuclear recoils over geological timescales could be used for studying astrophysical neutrinos, cosmic rays, dark matter and heavy exotic particles, as well as the variation of their fluxes over our Galaxy's lifetime. In recent years the international MDvDM community has been successfully tackling the challenges associated with realizing the concept of mineral detectors, opening the pathway towards a fully fledged experimental program and potential future discoveries.

arxiv:2609.13562.title: Direct detection of right-handed fermionic dark matter: electron-recoil measurements in Xe atoms
arxiv:2609.13562.abstract: We present theoretical estimations of the event rates for the interaction between a right-handed fermionic dark matter with an electron bound to a xenon atom. Motivated by recent astrophysical and cosmological constraints on a fermionic dark matter candidate in the sub-MeV mass range, we study such an interaction through an effective electromagnetic channel where the output consists of standard-model particles. This mechanism allows right-handed neutral dark matter fermions to couple with standard-model particles with the interchange of $W^{\pm}$ or $Z$ bosons, without the need to add extra fields. We generalize and extend previous results on this type of channels, by including for the ionization form factor arising from the interaction of the fermionic candidate with bound electrons. In addition, we compute the sensitivity curves for different direct detection experiments in such a challenging light particle mass range.

arxiv:2609.08483.title: News from NA61/SHINE
arxiv:2609.08483.abstract: NA61/SHINE is a multi-purpose, fixed-target hadron spectrometer at the CERN SPS. Its research program includes studies of strong interactions, as well as reference measurements for neutrino and cosmic-ray physics. A significant advantage of NA61/SHINE over collider experiments is its extended coverage of phase space available for particle production. This contribution summarizes recent selected results from our strong interaction program. These include rapidity spectra of K + and π − mesons in Xe+La reactions compared to other collision systems, energy dependence of the scaled π − total yield (the ‘kink’ plot) in Xe+La compared to other collision systems and models, ϕ(1020) rapidity spectra in Ar+Sc collisions compared to models, Λ transverse polarization in p + p reactions, energy dependence of intensive quantities of net-electric charge distribution in Ar+Sc collisions compared to p + p results, as well as an update on the evidence of large violation of isospin symmetry in kaon production — the excess of charged over neutral kaons.

doi:10.22323/1.511.0194.title: Investigation of Muon Excess from Initial Hadronic Interactions in Cosmic Air Showers with a One-ton Scintillator Detector at CJPL
doi:10.22323/1.511.0194.abstract: Over the past decade, ground-based array experiments have reported a notable deficit in simulated muons from extensive air showers (EAS) induced by high-energy cosmic rays, compared with experimental observations. This discrepancy is known as the \textit{muon puzzle}. In this work, we present the first study of this issue at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory (CJPL), where a 2400-m vertical rock overburden restricts muons to energies above 3 TeV, corresponding to an average primary cosmic-ray energy of about 0.4 PeV. This provides a clean window for probing the initial stages of EAS development. Using data collected over 1338.6 live days with the 1-ton prototype of the Jinping Neutrino Experiment, together with a GEANT4-based flux simulation framework, we perform a direct comparison between the measurement and predictions. Our results show that the observed muon flux is about 40% higher than post-LHC model expectations, offering new constraints for resolving the muon puzzle. These findings underscore the potential of deep underground environments for future high-energy cosmic-ray research.

arxiv:2608.16107.title: Unfolding the low-energy reactor neutrino flux from CE$ν$NS data with a finite Dirac sum
arxiv:2608.16107.abstract: We present a novel method to analyze coherent elastic neutrino--nucleus scattering (CE$ν$NS) data to extract the reactor antineutrino spectrum below the inverse beta decay threshold of 1.8 MeV, where it remains unmeasured. Adapting halo-independent analysis techniques developed for direct dark matter detection, we show how to obtain a best-fit and a pointwise confidence band for the integrated neutrino flux, without assuming a parametric form or smoothness prior for the spectrum. In our approach, which follows from convex geometry arguments, the differential neutrino rate is written as a linear combination of Dirac delta functions -- a finite Dirac sum (FDS) -- with a maximum number of terms determined by the number of data points. We apply our "FDS method" to mock CE$ν$NS data for a low-threshold Ge detector and compare it with Tikhonov-regularized unfolding.

arxiv:2608.12940.title: Newtrinos.jl: A Julia Package for Global Analysis of Neutrino Data
